weakness: The MAE alignment loss motivation (citing Park et al. 2023 that MAE captures high-frequency features) is asserted without the paper providing its own spectral analysis to verify this claim holds in the turbulence domain, and it is unclear which layers are aligned or whether the benefit comes from high-frequency guidance versus general regularization.
justification: Section 3.3 cites Park et al. for the high-frequency claim but presents no spectral verification specific to the fluid dynamics representations used, and does not analyze which alignment layers drive the effect beyond stating 'selected feature layers.'

weakness: The OOD generalization experiments (Figure 7) compare FourierFlow only against surrogate baselines, not against generative baselines like STDiT/CFM, so it's unclear whether generative baselines also generalize well.
justification: Section 5.4 and Figure 7's description state comparison is against 'the SOTA surrogate baseline' only; no generative baseline curves are mentioned in the OOD generalization results.

weakness: Hyperparameter choices for k=4 (generation horizon), eta (frequency weighting exponent), and neighborhood size (5 in SFA) are not justified or ablated, despite being non-trivial design decisions affecting model behavior.
justification: The paper states k is set to 4 (Section 2.1), eta is initialized as 1 (Section 3.2), and neighborhood is 5 by default (Section 3.2) with no accompanying ablation or justification for these specific values in the visible text.

weakness: No variance estimates (standard deviations) reported for any results in Tables 1 and 2, only means of five runs, making it hard to assess statistical robustness of close comparisons (e.g., LandUse21 0% MR: CorreGen 32.87 vs DIVIDE 32.50).
justification: The paper explicitly states 'All the results are the mean of five individual runs with different random seeds' (Table 1 caption) with no standard deviation reported anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: The noise ratio hyperparameter ρ used in the virtual sample mechanism is not explained in the main text — it's unclear whether it is tuned, set to the true synthetic noise ratio (giving an oracle advantage), or otherwise chosen.
justification: The main text introduces ρ in Eq. 12 (Section 3.2.1) only as 'the potential noise ratio' with no discussion of how its value is determined; the paper says construction details are in Appendix C but the main text truly leaves this unaddressed.

weakness: The claim that CorreGen 'consistently achieves the best performance' (Section 4.2) is overstated, since Table 2 shows CANDY beating CorreGen on ACC for Scene15 at 80% MR (42.27 vs 40.96).
justification: The paper's own Table 2 data (visible in the text) shows CorreGen's ACC of 40.96 on that MR/CR row while the review's cited CANDY figure is a case where the blanket 'consistently best' phrasing in Section 4.2 is not literally exact.

weakness: The GMM-guided marginal estimation in Eqs. 13-14 is a heuristic curve-shaping construction with two extra tuning parameters, not a standard probabilistic GMM posterior, undercutting the 'principled' framing of the method.
justification: The paper's own Eq. 13 applies a shaping transformation with hyperparameters distinct from the standard GMM posterior formula, matching the reviewer's technical description.

weakness: The category-level mismatch claim is not directly tested experimentally — only sample-level mismatch (MR/CR) is varied in the main experiments, with only indirect visualization evidence (Fig. 3) for category-level correspondence recovery.
justification: The paper itself acknowledges in Section 4.2 that 'category-level mismatch is an intrinsic challenge rather than one that can be explicitly specified' and relies on the posterior visualization as indirect support, confirming the reviewer's point.

weakness: Scaffold confound undermines model-level conclusions from the headline ranking, since each model is paired with a different scaffold chosen to maximize performance, yet conclusions are drawn as though scaffold were controlled.
justification: The paper itself states 'agent and model performance are hard to decouple' (line 235) and Figure 1's caption confirms 'the agent scaffold used to report each model was chosen to maximize performance,' supporting the reviewer's point.

weakness: The 'neutral testbed' claim for Terminus 2 is asserted without empirical support that it does not systematically favor or disfavor particular model families.
justification: The paper only justifies neutrality by simplicity ('Terminus 2 has a single tool... completes tasks using only Bash commands', line 237) without any evidence comparing rankings across scaffolds to support the neutrality claim.

weakness: Confidence intervals are mentioned in Figure 1's caption but never reported or discussed numerically in the text or tables.
justification: Line 65 states 'error bars correspond to a 95% confidence interval' but the results table (lines ~45-261) only lists point-estimate percentages with no CI values given anywhere.

weakness: No quantified breakdown of task rejection rates at each phase of the verification pipeline (229 submitted, 89 selected).
justification: Line 69 states 229 tasks were submitted and 89 selected 'based on the author's difficulty assessment and a quality assessment,' but no per-phase rejection counts are given in the visible text.

weakness: Qualifications of human reviewers are unspecified ('experienced' is vague) despite being central to the benchmark's quality claims.
justification: The paper repeatedly uses 'experienced human reviewers' / 'experienced task reviewers' (lines 69, 121, 177) without ever defining their domain expertise or background.

weakness: Task category imbalance (several categories with only 1-2 tasks) limits per-category analysis utility.
justification: Figure 4/Table (lines 202-225) confirms categories like Games (2), Video Processing (1), Data Querying (1), Optimization (1), Personal Assistant (1), supporting the claim.

weakness: Potential circularity in failure analysis using GPT-5 as judge for classifying failures of GPT-family models like GPT-5.2.
justification: Line 300 confirms 'GPT-5 (high-reasoning mode) serves as our primary judge' for failure analysis that includes GPT-5.2 among the evaluated models, and the paper does not discuss potential judge-family bias.

weakness: Weak evidence for the 'model selection is usually more important than agent scaffold' claim, based on only two non-systematic comparisons.
justification: Line 261 shows the claim is derived from exactly two comparisons (GPT-5.2 vs GPT-5-Nano on Codex CLI, and Gemini-2.5-Pro on Terminus 2 vs OpenHands), matching the reviewer's characterization of insufficient/non-systematic evidence.

weakness: Unexplained catastrophic failure on LLaMA-2-7B/PTB (PPL 3166 vs ARB-RC 763) contradicts claim of consistent improvement; paper dismisses it by saying the metric is meaningless while still claiming consistent outperformance in conclusion.
justification: The paper text confirms line 233 dismisses the 3166 PTB result as uninformative while the conclusion (Section 6) still asserts the method 'consistently outperforms prior 1-bit PTQ approaches,' which is an internal contradiction the review correctly identifies.

weakness: The selective-layer design choice (output alignment only on last FC layer of each block) is stated without ablation evidence comparing alternatives.
justification: Section 4.2 states the choice is made 'since it has the most direct impact on the block loss' but no ablation over alternative layer-selection strategies is presented in the visible text, supporting the review's claim.

weakness: The claim of 'minimal overhead' in the abstract is unsubstantiated in the main text, deferring all overhead analysis to Appendix D with only a one-line reference.
justification: Section 5.3 explicitly reads 'Overhead Analysis. Please refer to Appendix D' with no summary in the main text, confirming the review's claim.

weakness: The personalization vs. longer-context confound is not experimentally separated -- no ablation holds the context window fixed while isolating the personalization mechanism from the effect of a longer context window than ActionPiece uses.
justification: The paper's own Section 2.4 (line 208) acknowledges Pctx extends the perceived context window beyond adjacent actions, and Table 3's ablations do not include a controlled variant isolating context length from personalization, so this gap is genuine.

weakness: No variance or multi-run statistics reported -- Table 2 gives single numbers per method/metric with significance markers but no stated number of seeds/runs or standard deviations/confidence intervals.
justification: This is a factual observation about the paper's reporting; the paper does not state seed counts or report variance alongside its single-run results.

weakness: Tight coupling with the auxiliary DuoRec model is acknowledged but not critically examined as a current limitation, despite Table 3's SASRec ablation showing performance degrades substantially with a weaker context encoder.
justification: The reviewer notes the paper frames this only as future work ('end-to-end personalized action tokenizers') rather than discussing the dependency as a present limitation, which is a fair reading of the conclusion's framing.

weakness: Overstated 'two orders of magnitude' claim; actual best improvement is ~26x (~1.4 orders of magnitude), not ~100x
justification: Table 1 shows D-SCRIPT MAP@5 improves from 0.0103 to 0.2714 (~26x) and Recall@5 from 0.0071 to 0.1832 (~26x), well short of two orders of magnitude, yet the abstract and conclusion state 'two orders of magnitude'.

weakness: Missing ablation isolating whether improvement comes from known-partner-anchor retrieval alone vs. the contact-map active-region masking specifically (full-embedding cosine similarity baseline missing)
justification: The paper only compares against raw interaction probabilities (Table 1), which lack the anchor structure entirely; no baseline uses known-partner anchors with full-embedding similarity, so this gap is real.

weakness: Re-ranking analysis (Table 2) reports only direction of rank shift (maintained/improved vs worsened), not magnitude, and does not state how many of the 2,280 pairs are true positives
justification: Section 5.2/Table 2 description confirms only fraction maintained-or-improved vs worsened is reported, with no mean/median rank shift or count of true positives among the 2,280 pairs stated in the text.

weakness: No variance or confidence intervals reported for metrics in Table 1
justification: Table 1 and surrounding text present only single point estimates per metric/cutoff with no bootstrap or per-protein variance reported.

weakness: Comparison between the pipeline (which uses known partners as anchors) and raw baseline models (which don't use known partners) conflates the effect of the retrieval strategy with the effect of the underlying PPI model
justification: The baselines in Table 1 use only prediction probability; no baseline combines known-partner-aware retrieval with the raw PPI model's interaction probability, so this confound is real and not addressed in the paper.

weakness: Missing details on evaluation scope: paper does not state how many target proteins were evaluated or the distribution of novel partners per target, making it hard to know if aggregate metrics are driven by a few well-connected proteins
justification: Section 5.1 reports 279,568 additional positives in v12 but no per-target-protein counts or distribution of novel partners are given anywhere in the paper text provided.

weakness: Retrieval runtime described as 'hundreds of hours' but not contextualized for practical use or discussed in terms of possible approximations
justification: Section 5.3 states runtimes are 'in the order of hundreds of hours' with no further discussion of practicality or speedup strategies.

weakness: Unclear/unexplained difference in prediction coverage figures between D-SCRIPT's probability baseline (95.4%) and the proposed method (92.3%)
justification: Table 1 shows these two coverage values without any textual explanation of why the proposed method has lower coverage, so the trade-off is indeed unaddressed.

weakness: Zero baseline comparisons are reported despite three baselines being defined and RQ1 explicitly asking how HASTE performs compared to baselines.
justification: Section 4.1.3 (lines 154-156) defines IR-only, AST-only, and naive truncation baselines and RQ1 (line 124) asks about comparison to baselines, but Section 5 results only report HASTE's own scores/compression with no baseline numbers anywhere in the text.

weakness: Two of three defined evaluation metrics (AST Fidelity and Hallucination Rate) are never reported in the results.
justification: Sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.3 (lines 178-184) define AST Fidelity and Hallucination Rate, but Section 5 only discusses Judge Score, compression ratio, and correlation values -- neither metric appears in any table or figure.

weakness: The evaluation corpus is too small (6 curated files, 12 SWE-PolyBench instances from one repo) to support the paper's claims, and the r=-0.97 correlation is driven by a single outlier without CI/significance testing; excluded 'processing error' instances are unquantified.
justification: Lines 135, 207, and 213 confirm exactly 6 files, correlation computed on those 6 points driven by test3.py, and SWE-PolyBench evaluation 'excludes instances that resulted in processing errors' without stating how many or the criteria.

weakness: Key experimental parameters are unspecified: no numerical token budget is given, the embedding model is only described generically, and it's unclear whether Gemini 1.5 Flash serves as editor, judge, or both.
justification: Line 92 says only 'state-of-the-art transformer-based encoders' with no named model, 'strict token budget' is mentioned repeatedly (e.g. line 110) with no numeric value given, and line 164 states Gemini 1.5 Flash is the 'fixed underlying LLM' without clarifying its role relative to the judge described in 4.2.1.

weakness: The headline 85% compression claim is selectively reported, coming only from the test3.py outlier while other files show 1.2x-2.7x compression, and no average is reported.
justification: Line 203 attributes the 85.3% reduction/6.8x compression specifically to test3.py, while the compression ratios chart (line 234-245) shows the other five files ranging 1.2-2.7x, and no average across files is stated anywhere in Section 5.

weakness: No baselines in any main-text experiment; every experiment evaluates the Gram determinant score in isolation against ground-truth metrics (p, Hamming, l2), and any statistic correlated with corruption could show similar trends.
justification: Section 5's three experiments (lines 227-270) only report the Gram determinant score against p, Hamming distance, and l2 error; no alternative scoring method (e.g., trace of confusion matrix, entropy) appears anywhere in the main text.

weakness: Experiments do not directly test the strongest theoretical claim (Blackwell ordering preservation); the six corruption policies used are not verified to produce Q matrices satisfying the invertibility/diagonal-maximality conditions needed for Blackwell ordering.
justification: Theorem 4.2 part 2 requires Q, Q' in Q_reg (invertible, diagonally maximal), but Experiments 1-3 (lines 227-270) evaluate correlation with Hamming distance and p using ad-hoc corruption policies (uniform, asym neighbor, merge, etc.) without checking or ensuring Q_reg membership.

weakness: The dist-ordering guarantee (Theorem 4.2 part 3) is theoretically very narrow, requiring delta <= 1/(64L^2 d^2), permitting at most N/1600 misreports for d=5, L=1, and the paper does not sufficiently emphasize how restrictive this is.
justification: The condition Q_{L,1/64L^2d^2} in Theorem 4.2 (line 185) is exactly as restrictive as described; the paper states the condition explicitly but does not discuss its practical narrowness in the main text.

weakness: Computational cost of the plug-in estimator (O(N^2) pairwise comparisons) is not discussed anywhere in the paper, despite being significant for N=4000-10000.
justification: Definition 4.4's plug-in estimator sums over all pairs n,n' in [N], which is O(N^2); no discussion of this cost appears in Sections 4.2 or 5.

weakness: Employment data experiment (Experiment 3) lacks uncertainty quantification; with N=209 and d=4, no confidence intervals or standard errors are reported for Figure 3d.
justification: The description of Experiment 3 (lines 266-270) reports only point estimates of the score for three vintages without any mention of confidence intervals or standard errors, unlike Experiments 1-2 which report mean and standard error over M=100 trials.

weakness: The |Y| < d case (PᵀP full rank requirement, implicitly |Y| >= d) is not acknowledged as a limitation of the basic score.
justification: The factorization in Eq. 4 relies on det(PᵀP) being nonzero, which requires |Y| >= d, but the paper's discussion of Section 4.3 limitations (line 219) only mentions continuous Y and structural information, not the |Y| < d rank issue.

weakness: Threshold inconsistency: summary/introduction/abstract state the threshold as 'effective size below 8-bit 4B' for the eviction-vs-quantization choice (Finding 5), but Section 5's actual Finding 5 text and prose state the threshold as 'effective size smaller than an 8-bit 8B model.'
justification: Confirmed in paper text: line 49 says 'effective size smaller than an 8-bit 4B model' for KV eviction vs quantization, while lines 211 and 221 (Finding 5) explicitly say 'effective size smaller than an 8-bit 8B model.' This is a genuine internal inconsistency.

weakness: The budget-forcing method used to vary token budgets may confound Finding 1, since small models naturally terminate earlier and thus have a larger fraction of forced (possibly lower-quality) tokens, and the paper does not analyze or control for this.
justification: The paper describes budget forcing in Section 3 (line 91) but nowhere reports the fraction of forced tokens per model size or attempts to disentangle this from the memory-allocation conclusion in Finding 1.

weakness: Finding 2's claim that '4-bit is broadly memory-optimal for knowledge-intensive tasks' is generalized from a single benchmark, GPQA-Diamond, with no second knowledge-intensive benchmark to support the broader claim.
justification: The paper's task list (line 89) confirms only GPQA-Diamond represents knowledge-intensive reasoning, while AIME25, MATH500, and LiveCodeBench are math/code; no additional knowledge benchmark like MMLU-Pro is used.

weakness: The 'effective size' hypothesis (that behavior is governed by N x bits, not N and bits separately) is not tested by comparing different N/bit combinations that yield the same effective size (e.g., 2B-16bit vs 4B-4bit); the additional model families tested (R1-Distill, Nemotron) offer different N values rather than isolating this factor.
justification: The paper defines effective size (line 73) and claims it 'mainly governs' behavior (line 43), but the described experiments (Section 3, Table 1) vary N and bits together within each family without a controlled comparison isolating effective size from N/precision separately.

weakness: Tension between strong practical claims (glvLiNG as 'efficient algorithm', 'first structural-assumption-free discovery method') and the paper's own admission that glvLiNG is 'more as a proof of concept' due to OICA's known inefficiency in practice.
justification: Paper text confirms both the strong claims (abstract, contribution 4) and the 'proof of concept'/'OICA's known inefficiency' framing in Final Remarks, so the tension is real and grounded.

weakness: The linear programming baseline used for the runtime comparison is not described in enough detail to judge its validity, making the runtime speedup claim unverifiable in the main text.
justification: Paper only states 'We compare the execution time against a linear programming baseline for constructing digraphs to satisfy ranks of oracle OICA mixing matrices' with no further description of its formulation in the main text.

weakness: The oracle comparison against LaHiCaSi and PO-LiNGAM only tests them under assumption violations, without a complementary evaluation under assumption-matched conditions to see if glvLiNG loses performance by being more general.
justification: Paper explicitly frames the comparison as testing baselines under structural misspecification ('how existing methods behave under structural misspecification'), and no main-text experiment under matched assumptions is described.

weakness: Main-text evaluation (Section 5) is thin for a method claimed as a co-equal contribution, providing only brief qualitative summaries with key numbers but no tables/figures in the main paper.
justification: Section 5 text gives only numeric summaries (783 classes, n=10 under 5s, misidentify over half of edges) with 'Full results/statistics' deferred to appendix tables (Table 3, 4, 5).

weakness: Equivalence class enumeration reports counts (e.g., 783 equivalence classes) but not informativeness, i.e., whether classes are mostly singleton or large multi-graph classes.
justification: The paper reports only class counts and sizes in Table 3 without discussing the distribution of class sizes or their implications for identification uncertainty.

weakness: Faithfulness robustness under near-violations (finite-sample rank estimation error, near-cancellations) is not discussed; the formal faithfulness assumption is deferred to the appendix.
justification: Paper defers the faithfulness assumption to 'Assumption 1 at Appendix A' and provides no discussion of near-violation robustness in the main text.

weakness: MSE-Bench evaluation relies on GPT-4o judge with no human agreement study or calibration reported, making the 48.7% Turn-5 success rate hard to interpret.
justification: The paper explicitly states (line 122-123) it uses GPT-4o to judge success with no mention of any human validation or agreement study anywhere in the text.

weakness: Data scaling results (Fig. 5) flatline from 2.5M to 10M contradicting the claimed 'nearly log-linear' trend, and there is a numerical discrepancy between the abstract (5% to 22%) and the main text (Table 2 reports 25% at 10M).
justification: Line 239 claims a 'nearly log-linear increase' for later turns, while line 165 reports the final Turn-5 success rate as 25%, which does not match the abstract's stated endpoint of 22% (line 29), confirming a real numerical inconsistency.

weakness: The core proxy-task ablation (Table 3) uses an intermediate, not fully trained, checkpoint, limiting the conclusiveness of the central methodological contribution.
justification: The paper's own footnote on Table 3 states this ablation was conducted using an intermediate checkpoint and numbers may not be directly comparable to other tables, confirming the criticism is accurate and paper-acknowledged.

weakness: VINCIE underperforms on CLIP-T (instruction-following) on MagicBrush relative to several baselines, a pattern the paper does not discuss.
justification: Table 1 shows Ours(7B+SFT) CLIP-T of 0.283 at Turn-1 vs 0.292-0.293 for GPT Image 1/Qwen-Image-Edit, and the surrounding text (line 163) only emphasizes outperforming 'nearly all metrics' without acknowledging this CLIP-T gap.

weakness: No evaluation variance (confidence intervals/multiple runs) is reported for the stochastic GPT-4o-based MSE-Bench evaluation, despite only 100 test instances.
justification: The paper reports point-estimate success rates in Table 2 without any variance, CI, or repeated-run statistics for the GPT-4o judged benchmark.

weakness: MSE-Bench contains only 100 test instances, making results sensitive to individual cases and lacking confidence intervals.
justification: This is consistent with the paper's benchmark description and the same underlying gap as the variance-reporting issue; no sample-size justification or CI is given in the text.

weakness: The 'Tensor Field Network' (TFN) component is a pointwise quadratic transformation with no spatial convolution, no spherical-harmonic features, no Clebsch-Gordan tensor products, and no type-l representations, unlike the actual Tensor Field Networks (Thomas et al., 2018) it is named after and cites.
justification: Eq. 3.2 (line 75) confirms f_TFN(I[i,c_out]) = sum W[c_out,c1,c2](I[i,c1]*I[i,c2]) applied per-index i, a purely pointwise operation, which does not match the spatial-kernel-based equivariance mechanism of real TFNs.

weakness: The paper's own tables (Table 1 and Table 2) contain multiple cases where PA-TFNP underperforms ClimODE or other baselines, contradicting the 'consistently outperforms' narrative, and the headline 78.92%/38.12% improvement numbers are never defined or derived.
justification: Line 156 states the aggregate percentages with no definition of computation, while Table 1 (lines 168-190) and Table 2 (lines 202-217) show specific per-variable losses to baselines, supporting the reviewer's claim.

weakness: The evaluation omits comparisons against SOTA models the paper itself cites as state-of-the-art (FourCastNet, Pangu-Weather, GraphCast), despite the abstract claiming 'state-of-the-art performance.'
justification: Line 31 discusses FourCastNet, Pangu-Weather, and GraphCast as state-of-the-art, but line 144 shows experiments only compare against NODE, ClimaX, and ClimODE.

weakness: Parameter counts and computational-resource/efficiency claims (comparable parameters, fewer computational resources) are made but never substantiated with parameter counts, FLOPs, or wall-clock comparisons.
justification: Abstract and intro (lines 9, 19) make these claims, but the only hardware mention (line 144, 'a single RTX 4090 GPU') provides no comparative efficiency data anywhere in the text.

weakness: The ablation study (TFNP vs. PA-TFNP) bundles five distinct components together with no component-wise breakdown, making it unclear which modification drives the improvement.
justification: Section 4.4 (lines 217-223) only compares the aggregate TFNP and PA-TFNP models without isolating boundary conditions, spherical gradient correction, physics features, diffusion, or momentum correction individually.

weakness: Section 4.1 describes the 5.625° grid as 'coarse' and the 11.25° grid as 'finer', which is backwards since 5.625° has more grid points and is actually the finer resolution.
justification: Line 148 literally states 'coarse resolution (5.625°)' and 'finer resolution (11.25°)', which is inverted since a smaller degree spacing corresponds to a finer grid.

weakness: Empirical margins are small (1.40% average, MBPP margin only 0.14%) and paper reports 'averaged over three runs' but provides no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests.
justification: Table 1 caption (line 176) confirms 'results averaged over three runs' but no variance/error bars or significance tests appear anywhere in the paper text.

weakness: LLM-as-Judge used for candidate selection without validating that its scores correlate with actual task performance.
justification: Line 152 describes the LLM-as-judge scoring candidates on 'semantic fit, structure, and task relevance' but no correlation analysis with rollout performance is presented anywhere in the paper.

weakness: Imprecise language conflating Mermaid-graph-level validity guarantees with actual Python code correctness guarantees, since Python translation succeeds only >90% of the time.
justification: Lines 90/152 use strong terms like 'guaranteed to be syntactically valid, type-safe, and structurally executable' while line 201 admits only '>90% success rate in producing valid Python code', confirming the imprecision.

weakness: Unnecessary and hard-to-substantiate 'first' claims (e.g., 'first agentic workflow framework to guarantee static graph-level correctness').
justification: The paper does make exactly these claims verbatim (lines 30, 78, 285) without engaging with how prior structured frameworks like MetaGPT or GPTSwarm compare.

weakness: No explanation of how the initial valid graph G0 is obtained, despite the induction argument in Section 4.1 assuming G0 is in S.
justification: Line 134 states 'Given an initial graph G0 ∈ S' but the paper text does not describe the concrete process for producing this first valid graph.

weakness: Duplicated paragraph appears at line 201 and line 211 (copy-paste error about >90% success rate).
justification: Verified directly in the paper text: the identical sentence about '>90% success rate in producing valid Python code' and token efficiency appears twice, at lines 201 and 211.

weakness: Crossover probability (10%) is not ablated or justified despite being the showcased operation in Figure 4.
justification: Line 168 states crossover is applied with 'only a 10% probability' for 'experimental stability' but no ablation study varying this value is presented.

weakness: Token efficiency comparison (2.7e4 vs 6.9e4 tokens) does not specify what types of tokens are counted or whether it controls for number of candidates generated.
justification: Line 201 reports the token figures without any breakdown of token categories (generation, judge, evaluation) or normalization details.

weakness: No variance or uncertainty reported for any quantitative result (no standard errors, CIs, or multi-seed runs) across Tables 1, 2, 4, 5.
justification: The paper reports single point-estimate AUROC/pass@1 values throughout the tables with no mention of seeds, error bars, or confidence intervals in the visible text.

weakness: Stage II analysis lacks a critical control: contamination without CoT to isolate whether detection failure is CoT-specific or a general property of capable LRMs.
justification: The paper's Stage II discussion (Section 4) argues CoT-driven generalization causes detection failure but does not include an ablation contaminating LRMs with non-CoT QA pairs to isolate the cause.

weakness: Stage I ecological validity is overstated: for Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, SFT contamination alone (47.23 avg pass@1) outperforms SFT contamination followed by clean RL (45.55), undermining the motivating narrative that RL is used to conceal.
justification: Table 1 confirms exactly these numbers (47.23 for 'Clean & Mem / /' vs 45.55 for 'Clean & Mem / Clean'), and the paper does not explain why a developer would accept this score reduction.

weakness: The 'broad class of RL methods' claim is broader than the evidence, since only GRPO and RAFT++ (both PPO-style) are tested, not PPO itself, DPO, or Reinforce.
justification: The paper explicitly tests RAFT, RAFT++, and GRPO only (Table 3, Section 3.2) and extrapolates via mechanism to a 'broad class of RL methods' without testing other algorithms.

weakness: 'Theorem 3.1' overstates rigor since it is a first-order expansion relying on qualitative claims about covariance term signs/magnitudes rather than formal bounds or proofs of gap contraction.
justification: The stated Theorem 3.1 (Eq. 5) is a small-step expansion, and the subsequent derivations (e.g., 'Empirically, the covariance gap offsets...', 'is much more prominent... due to high variance') rely on qualitative/empirical reasoning rather than formal proofs of the claimed inequality.

weakness: Factual error: paper calls DeepSeek-V3 the overall best-performing model despite it scoring 32.60, second-lowest in Table 1
justification: Line 265 explicitly states DeepSeek-V3 'can thus be regarded as the overall best-performing model' while Table 1 shows DeepSeek-V3 at 32.60, well below the 39.08 average and GPT-5's 47.28 - a direct internal contradiction.

weakness: Missing correlation analysis between LPFQA rankings and existing benchmarks like MMLU/HLE to validate distinctness of the benchmark
justification: The paper nowhere reports a correlation/rank analysis against MMLU, HLE, or Arena-Hard; this is a real, verifiable omission relevant to benchmark validation.

weakness: Circularity in post-hoc filtering procedure using the same 12 evaluated models to filter questions then re-evaluating those same models
justification: Section 4.2.1 confirms the same 12 models used for evaluation are used to filter to LPFQA- and LPFQA=, and the paper does not address or mitigate this circularity anywhere in the text.

weakness: Unsupported conclusion that code interpreter results show LPFQA reflects knowledge not reasoning ability is a non-sequitur
justification: Section 4.2.2 draws the causal conclusion 'LPFQA primarily reflects a model's mastery of domain knowledge rather than its reasoning ability' from a single ablation without ruling out alternative explanations like poor tool integration, which the paper does not address.

weakness: Unsupported conclusion that search tool decline reflects long-tail retrieval difficulty rather than alternatives like poor query formulation
justification: Section 4.2.2 attributes the drop to retrieval difficulty of long-tail knowledge without evidence distinguishing this from query formulation or integration failures.

weakness: Per-field conclusions drawn from tiny sample sizes (e.g., DS=3, AI=8, Aero=8) without confidence intervals
justification: Figure 2 and Section 3.3 confirm these small per-field counts, and Section 4.1 draws specific claims like 'GPT-5 shows clear superiority in Phys and AI' without reporting any variance measures anywhere in the paper.

weakness: Missing construction pipeline details: MLLM/LLM used for generation/cleaning not named, expert verification details absent, difficulty-test models unnamed
justification: Sections 3.2.2 and 3.2.3 only say 'MLLM', 'an LLM', and 'Multiple LLMs' without naming them or giving expert count/qualifications, confirming the omission.

weakness: Inconsistency between abstract (502 tasks) and body (505 questions)
justification: Abstract line 9 says 'covering 502 tasks' while Section 3.1 and Figure 2 caption say 505 questions, a genuine numeric discrepancy.

weakness: No qualitative or error analysis of what kinds of errors models make despite four evaluation dimensions
justification: The paper reports aggregate scores per dimension/field but nowhere provides a breakdown of error types or qualitative analysis of failure modes.

weakness: No statistical dispersion (standard deviations/confidence intervals) reported despite averaging over three trials
justification: Line 211 states results are averaged over three trials, but Tables 1-4 report only point estimates with no variance measures.

weakness: BC-MLP (and RATE) achieving ~70% success on T-Maze at 1M steps is unexplained, suggesting the benchmark may leak information or have exploitable statistical bias, undermining the paper's headline horizon-extension claims.
justification: The paper does not discuss why a memory-free MLP baseline reaches 70% success on a task meant to require long-range memory recall; this gap is not addressed anywhere in the text.

weakness: The 'extends effective horizons up to 100,000 times' headline claim is only demonstrated on the synthetic T-Maze, while realistic MIKASA-Robo results (RememberColor5/9) are near chance level, and the 70% aggregate improvement figure is not verifiable from the main paper text.
justification: Table 1 shows RememberColor9-v0 success of only 0.23±0.02 for ELMUR, and the aggregate figure is deferred to Appendix Table 8 which is not included in the reviewed text, so the strong abstract claim cannot be checked against the main paper.

weakness: Inconsistency in MIKASA-Robo task count: the paper says ELMUR ranks first on 21 of 23 tasks in the abstract/intro, but the Table 1 caption references 'all 32 MIKASA-Robo tasks'.
justification: Confirmed directly: line 9/27 state '21 of 23 tasks' while line 236 (Table 1 caption) states 'all 32 MIKASA-Robo tasks in Appendix, Table 8', an unresolved numerical inconsistency.

weakness: Theoretical analysis (Propositions 1 and 2, effective horizon formula) is basic and never instantiated with the actual λ and M used in the T-Maze experiment, so it is disconnected from the empirical results.
justification: The paper presents the effective horizon formula but the experimental setup section (line 204) and ablation (line 261) do not report the specific λ/M used for the T-Maze 1M-step result or verify the formula's prediction against it.

weakness: Hyperparameter values (M, λ, σ, L, S, D_max) for each benchmark are deferred to the appendix rather than reported in the main paper, hurting reproducibility.
justification: The main text experimental setup (line 204) describes L and S generically for T-Maze but does not tabulate per-benchmark hyperparameter values, which the review notes are needed for evaluating the effective-horizon claims.

weakness: POPGym aggregate scores (Table 2) lack error bars/standard errors, unlike individual task means, making it impossible to assess whether ELMUR's aggregate advantage over RATE is statistically meaningful.
justification: The review's specific claim about missing standard errors on the aggregate rows is a concrete, checkable formatting/reporting gap not contradicted by the paper text provided.

weakness: The relative bias clamping to [-D_max+1, D_max-1] is not discussed as a limitation, even though it means the model cannot distinguish events beyond D_max steps in the past, which matters for the long-horizon claims.
justification: Line 118 confirms the clamping mechanism exists, but the paper does not discuss its implications for very-long-horizon retention as a limitation.

weakness: MoE-FFN vs MLP-FFN ablation shows MLP-FFN preserves accuracy while being more efficient, so the paper's choice of MoE-FFN is not well justified.
justification: Line 261 confirms 'replacing MoE-FFN with MLP-FFN preserves accuracy while improving computational efficiency,' yet the paper does not justify retaining the more complex MoE-FFN design.

weakness: The CartPole result (all methods reaching 500/500) is a trivial sanity check that provides no information about memory behavior and should be de-emphasized.
justification: This is a fair, well-grounded observation about the diagnostic value of a specific reported result rather than a vague or out-of-scope critique.

weakness: Structural gap between theoretical assumptions (four mutually independent sequences) and practical implementation (odd-even splitting yields only two sequences), and the paper does not quantify how much guarantees degrade under this violation.
justification: Paper explicitly states at line 89 that Stage I and Stage II 'are implemented using the same two split tensor sequences via the odd-even splitting approach' while Algorithm 1 and Theorems 1/2 require four mutually independent sequences; the paper offers no quantification of degradation from this gap.

weakness: Main-text baseline comparisons (gSeg, kerSeg) are not designed for multilayer networks, and the most relevant comparison (Wang et al. 2025, deep learning baselines) is deferred to the appendix.
justification: The paper confirms in Section 4.1 that comparisons with Wang et al. (2025) and Li et al. (2024) are reported in Appendix G.1, while the main text (Table 1, Table 3) only compares against gSeg and kerSeg.

weakness: The practical threshold choice τ=0.1n√L log^{3/2}(T) satisfies the lower bound of Theorem 1's condition but not verifiably the upper bound (which depends on unknown κ²Δ).
justification: Theorem 1 requires c_{τ,1}nsqrt(L)log^{3/2}(T) < τ < c_{τ,2}κ²Δ, and the paper's practical choice (Section 4.1, τ=c_{τ,1}n√L log^{3/2}(T)) only addresses the lower bound; κ and Δ are unknown in practice, and the paper does not prove the upper bound holds for the chosen τ.

weakness: Real-data confidence intervals in Table 4 for 2005 and 2013 detections do not contain the reported point estimates (time points 20 and 28), which is unusual and unexplained.
justification: Table 4 shows time point 20 with CI (17.97, 18.05) and time point 28 with CI (25.99, 26.06) -- neither interval contains the reported time point, and the paper gives no explanation for this discrepancy.

weakness: Table 1 reports only means over 100 Monte Carlo trials with no standard errors or variability measures, making it impossible to assess statistical significance of differences between methods.
justification: Table 1 in the paper indeed lists only mean values across methods/scenarios with no SE, variance, or CI columns.

weakness: Remark 1's comparison of offline vs. online localization rates conflates settings with fundamentally different information constraints, making the 'substantially sharper rate' framing misleading since no other offline method exists for direct comparison.
justification: Remark 1 explicitly compares the offline rate κ_k^{-2}log(T) against Wang et al. (2025)'s online rate without acknowledging that offline and online settings have different information availability, supporting this critique.

weakness: CI coverage evaluation (Table 2) is shown only for n=100 and n=150, while the main detection experiments (Table 1) include n=50, so CI performance at the smaller node size used for detection is not reported.
justification: Table 1 covers n∈{50,100} while Table 2 covers n∈{100,150}; the paper never reports CI coverage for n=50, confirming the gap.

weakness: No measure of uncertainty (standard errors, confidence intervals) is reported for any benchmark score in Tables 2 and 3; only point estimates from single runs per instance are given.
justification: The paper reports only averaged scores (Section 4.1: 'averaging the scores of the individual runs') with no dispersion measures in Tables 2 or 3, and the single Welch's t-test only tests the coarse difficulty-scaling hypothesis, not per-score reliability.

weakness: The pricing benchmark's validity as a test of economic reasoning is unclear, since GPT-4.1 outperforms GPT-5 and the paper's own analysis suggests agents rely on simple heuristics rather than genuine adaptation.
justification: The paper itself calls this 'surprising' (Section 4.2) and states most agents 'set prices using simple heuristics' and fail to 'adapt to, or sometimes even detect, changes' (Section 4.3), without providing further explanation, supporting the reviewer's concern.

weakness: The paper's claim of uncovering 'mechanisms' in Section 4.3 overstates what the descriptive correlations (budget utilization, best-so-far rate) actually establish, since causation is not shown.
justification: Section 4.3 only reports correlational observations (e.g., 'can likely be explained by,' 'we observe a close correspondence') without any causal analysis, matching the reviewer's critique of overstated 'mechanisms' language.

weakness: No non-LLM baselines are provided for the procurement and pricing environments, unlike scheduling which has a uniform random baseline.
justification: The paper's scoring formulas show procurement and pricing normalized only by OPT, while scheduling explicitly normalizes against 'uniform random matching' (Section 3.3.2), confirming the asymmetry the reviewer identifies.

weakness: The sample size of n=12 instances per condition is not justified in the paper.
justification: Section 4.1 states 'we randomly generate 12 instances' without any justification or reliability analysis for this choice, and Section 3.4 only notes that 'arbitrarily many' instances are possible in principle.

weakness: Qualitative annotation methodology is under-described (Section 2.3) — no detail on number of annotators, independence, or inter-rater reliability.
justification: The paper states only that the authors 'manually annotated' responses and 'publicly posted' the annotations (line 94), with no description of annotator count or reliability checks, confirming the gap.

weakness: The '3 of 4 ICLR 2025 reviewers and the Area Chair' claim (Section 5) is unsupported by citation.
justification: Line 204 makes this exact claim with no citation or link to the reviews, so the review's request for a source is well-grounded.

weakness: Uncertainty quantification (confidence intervals) is missing from the hyperparameter sweep results in Figure 5.
justification: The paper's description of Figure 5 (lines 159-163) reports only point-estimate differences ('Best Min-p - Best Other Sampler') with no confidence intervals, unlike Figure 1 and Figure 6 which do show CIs, confirming the described gap.

weakness: The hyperparameter ranges across samplers (e.g., min-p vs top-p) may not be equally informative, and the paper does not discuss this despite noting the ranges were adjusted.
justification: Line 133 confirms the paper only states values were 'lightly edited to make them more evenly distributed' without further justifying comparability of the ranges' informativeness.

weakness: The selective reporting claim in Section 4.3 relies on an external Telegram reference rather than a self-contained table.
justification: The paper does cite specific numbers (52.01 vs 50.14, etc.) but sources them via an external communication channel rather than including the full underlying data table, matching the review's observation.

weakness: No uncertainty quantification (confidence intervals, standard deviations, error bars) is reported for any of the main results in Tables 1, 2, 4, 5, or 7, despite multiple sources of variance (sampling randomness, GPU timing noise, correctness-check input randomness).
justification: Checking the paper text, none of the tables (1,2,4,5,6,7) report any variance measure, confidence interval, or number of repeated runs; results are reported as single point estimates throughout.

weakness: The paper never discusses the relationship/overlap between the training data source (KernelBook, used for PyTorch tasks in Section 3.3) and the evaluation benchmark (KernelBench), leaving open whether evaluation tasks were effectively seen during training.
justification: Section 3.3 states tasks were drawn from KernelBook and Section 4.2 evaluates on KernelBench, but no passage anywhere in the paper addresses overlap or disjointness between these two sources.

weakness: The abstract and contributions use causal language ("result in robust generation", "lead to reliable and robust kernel generation") that overstates what is actually a correlational/observational finding between conciseness and correctness.
justification: The paper text (Section 3.4, Abstract, contribution 1) does use exactly this causal phrasing while the underlying evidence (Figure 2, Figure 3, Pearson correlation) is observational/correlational, supporting the reviewer's point.

weakness: The claim of outperforming all frontier and fine-tuned models is stated without qualification even though KernelCoder trails DeepSeek-R1-0528 on the Level 1 fast1 pass@1 metric (17.0 vs 18.0 in Table 1).
justification: Table 1 confirms DeepSeek-R1-0528 CUDA has fast1=18.0 vs KernelCoder's 17.0 at Level 1, while the abstract/intro claim broad superiority without this caveat.

weakness: The individual contribution of task-type balancing (part (c) of the curation pipeline) is not isolated in the ablation study, since none of the 5K-random/max/min/speedup baselines control for task-type balance.
justification: Section 5.1 confirms the four ablation baselines only vary the selection criterion (random/max/min/speedup) and the text itself notes they "do not balance the types of tasks," so the isolated effect of part (c) is indeed untested.

weakness: The ARL-based difficulty division (Section 6) is partially self-validating because the difficulty measure and training data are both derived from Kevin-32B generations.
justification: Section 6.2 confirms Kevin was used as the ARL generator, the same model used to build ConCuR, which is a legitimate circularity concern even though the paper partially mitigates it by also showing the trend holds for DeepSeek-R1-0528.

weakness: The Figure 2 scatter plot analysis of reasoning length vs. speedup is dominated by low-speedup points, and a restricted analysis on kernels with speedup > 1 (the curation pipeline's target region) would be more informative.
justification: Figure 2's description confirms a dense cloud concentrated at low speedups (0.0-1.6 range) with R-squared=0.002 computed over the full range, supporting the reviewer's specific suggestion, though the reviewer itself notes the conclusion likely would not change.

weakness: No backbone-controlled baseline (e.g., Swin-B + GAP + concatenation + linear classifier), so it's impossible to isolate module contribution from backbone upgrade.
justification: The ablation table only removes GALP/Experts/LGRF individually while keeping Swin-B; no simple Swin-B baseline with naive fusion is reported anywhere in the paper, so the claim is well grounded.

weakness: No statistical significance or error bars for any result across Tables 1-4 and Fig. 3.
justification: All reported numbers in the tables and figures are single-point values; there is no mention of multiple seeds, std, or confidence intervals anywhere in the paper.

weakness: No qualitative validation (heatmap overlays, comparison to lesion masks, failure cases) that CAM proposals correspond to actual lesions.
justification: The paper describes GALP's CAM-derived proposals only mathematically (Eqs 1-7) and never shows visual/qualitative evidence connecting them to lesion segmentation masks, despite MFIDDR providing such masks.

weakness: Training hyperparameters (learning rate, optimizer, batch size, epochs, weight decay, schedule, augmentation) are largely unreported.
justification: The Implementation details paragraph only specifies backbone, pretraining, patch size, and loss weights; none of the listed training hyperparameters appear in the paper.

weakness: No statement about whether hyperparameter analysis (Fig. 3) used a validation split versus test set, raising concern of test-set tuning.
justification: The paper reports Fig. 3 results without mentioning any validation split, and the official splits described are only train/test, supporting this concern.

weakness: GALP ablation conflates the auxiliary loss with Top-K selection, since 'w/o GALP' removes both simultaneously.
justification: Section 4.3 explicitly states 'w/o GALP removes the GALP mechanism and directly uses all tokens for LGRF fusion,' confirming both the auxiliary loss and Top-K selection are removed together without disentangling their individual effects.

weakness: The LGRF 'corroboration' claim is interpretive storytelling rather than architecturally enforced, since routing (Eq. 9) is based on the current view's own features, not any cross-view agreement signal.
justification: Eq. 9 shows the Router takes only mean(F^i_sn) (current view's own tokens) as input, with no explicit comparison/agreement mechanism against the adjacent view's features, supporting the critique that 'corroboration' is not architecturally guaranteed.

weakness: No efficiency or complexity analysis (inference time, FLOPs, parameter counts) despite the paper claiming the method is 'scalable'.
justification: The conclusion claims the method is 'label-efficient and scalable,' but no FLOPs, latency, or parameter counts appear anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The 93% GNN accuracy conflates paper identity with a genuine semantic fingerprint, since node-level title embeddings act as near-unique identifiers of different papers, so the result may reflect content selection differences rather than a citation-pattern fingerprint.
justification: The paper never disentangles paper identity from stylistic/pattern signal in the node-level GNN setup (Section 6); it only reports the cross-generator RF result (~0.72) as a partial mitigation, so the concern about the 93% figure being confounded by paper identity is well-grounded and not addressed by an explicit control.

weakness: The paper's claim in Section 1 that structural features 'do not separate (i) from (ii) at statistically significant levels' is factually incorrect, since the reported accuracy (0.6079 ± 0.0058) is statistically significant even though the effect size is small.
justification: Table 1 reports mean accuracy 0.6079 ± 0.0058 across many graphs, whose CI clearly excludes 0.5, contradicting the paper's own 'not statistically significant' phrasing in Section 1.

weakness: The GNN structural node features include the graph's total edge count as a per-node feature, meaning every node in a graph receives the same scalar, introducing a graph-size confound.
justification: The paper text explicitly confirms this: 'consisting of degree centrality, closeness centrality, eigenvector centrality, clustering coefficient, and the graph's total number of edges, which is a graph level features but here assigned as node feature in GNN training,' matching the reviewer's description exactly.

weakness: Potential cross-focal-paper data leakage is not addressed: a paper could appear as a ground-truth reference for one focal paper and a GPT-suggested reference for another, and if such shared papers land in different splits, the GNN could memorize embedding-to-label mappings.
justification: The paper only describes controlling splits so that 'if a ground truth focal paper appeared in the train dataset, its respective random graph also appeared in the same split set' (Section 6), with no mention of controlling for reference-level overlap across different focal papers, so this gap is real.

weakness: The paper defers entirely to Algaba et al. (2025) for the verification rate of GPT-suggested references against SciSciNet, without reporting what fraction of GPT-4o's and Claude's suggested references could be verified or whether removed-graph counts (779 vs 89) indicate differing hallucination rates.
justification: Section 3 states 'The existence of the LLM-generated references is determined by cross-verification with the SciSciNet database... For more details, we refer to Algaba et al. (2025)' and gives removal counts (779 vs 89) without discussing what they imply, confirming the paper does not report this statistic itself.

weakness: The abstract/introduction claim that WGDT with a single click outperforms fully automatic methods is overclaimed as a headline result, since any click-based method provides a free spatial prior and WGDT vs. ADT/Disk (Section 4.1) is the more informative comparison.
justification: The paper does present the comparison to automatic baselines (Section 4.2, Figure 5) as a headline result in the abstract, while the paper itself never controls for the 'any click helps' confound; this is a legitimate framing critique.

weakness: Evaluation uses only simulated clicks, with no human annotator study, which weakens practical significance claims and is not discussed as a limitation in Section 5.
justification: Section 2.2 confirms clicks are entirely simulated, and Section 5's limitations paragraph discusses generalization to other regions, hyperparameter tuning, and noisy anatomy, but does not mention the simulation-only nature of the evaluation.

weakness: Per-sulcus modeling (training a separate binary model for each of 17 sulci) limits scalability to whole-cortex deployment, and the paper does not discuss the practical implications of this design choice.
justification: Section 2.1 confirms per-sulcus models are trained, and Section 5 only briefly mentions joint modeling as future work without discussing training/tuning/inference overhead implications.

weakness: The masking strategy in Section 3.3 (keeping only faces with curv >= 0) is ambiguous about whether it is applied uniformly to all compared methods including automatic baselines, which could affect Dice scores.
justification: Section 3.3 describes the masking generically without specifying whether automatic baselines undergo the same masking, so the ambiguity is real and could materially affect the Dice comparisons in Figure 5.

weakness: The loss function notation in Equation 6, log(p_n, z_n), is non-standard/ambiguous for cross-entropy loss and should be corrected.
justification: Equation 6 in the paper indeed uses the notation log(p_n, z_n), which is non-standard two-argument notation for cross-entropy loss, confirming the reviewer's observation.

weakness: BSDS500 edge detection reports a non-standard truncated metric (AP for recall < 20%) as the primary result without standard ODS/OIS F-measure in the main text, potentially inflating the 'crisper boundaries than SAM' claim.
justification: The paper itself states (line 227) 'We report AP for recall less than 20%... We explain this choice (and display the full precision-recall curves) in Appendix B' — confirming the main text only shows the truncated metric, supporting the reviewer's point.

weakness: The DINO baseline uses a non-standard decoder (frozen VAE via simple up-conv) that confounds architecture and pretraining, making the attribution of poor DINO performance to discriminative pretraining questionable.
justification: The paper (line 187) confirms DINO-B is paired with 'a frozen VAE decoder (from Stable Diffusion) via a simple up-conv,' which is indeed not a standard DINO segmentation architecture (e.g. CutLER, ViTDet), so the confound the reviewer raises is grounded in the paper's own described setup.

weakness: Multi-point promptable results are described (iterative multi-prompt protocol) but only single-point results are reported in the main text.
justification: Table 1 (line 148) reports 'zero-shot mIoU at a single prompt point' and no multi-point (1,2,5-point) results appear in the extracted text, matching the reviewer's claim that this analysis is missing.

weakness: The binarization threshold for the point-prompting similarity map is not specified, and it is unclear whether it is fixed or tuned per dataset, which affects reproducibility.
justification: Line 158 says the method 'threshold[s] the merged similarity map to produce the binary mask' without stating the threshold value, confirming this gap.

weakness: The hyperparameters lambda_sep and lambda_mean in the loss equation are mentioned but their values are not reported in the main text.
justification: Line 131 introduces lambda_sep and lambda_mean as 'hyperparameters controlling the importance of each loss term' without stating their numeric values anywhere in the visible main text.

weakness: SOTA claim not supported because most relevant prior language-guided dexterous manipulation work (HOIGPT, SemGrasp, AffordDexGrasp, DexGrasp Anything) discussed in related work is never used as a baseline comparison.
justification: Section 2.2 explicitly discusses HOIGPT as the most comparable prior work extending token-based generation to 3D HOI, yet Table 1/2/3 only compare against human whole-body motion models (TM2T, MDM, FlowMDM, MotionGPT3), confirming the gap.

weakness: Applying UniHM's own physics refinement to baselines confounds the comparison, only isolating the VLM difference rather than a fair end-to-end comparison.
justification: Line 257 states baselines are post-processed with UniHM's own refinement module, which the paper itself frames as ensuring fairness but actually only isolates one component, supporting the reviewer's methodological critique.

weakness: MPJPE, FOL, FPL are categorized as 'Physically Feasible' metrics but are actually trajectory-similarity metrics to human demonstration, not direct feasibility measures (no penetration, force-closure, or joint-limit metrics reported in simulation).
justification: Section 4.2 indeed labels these metrics under 'Physically Feasible' while their definitions (position/orientation error vs GT) are distance-to-demonstration metrics; the paper reports no penetration/force-closure metrics, confirming the mismatch.

weakness: Real-world evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no trial counts, confidence intervals, error bars, hand specification, or number of objects reported for Table 3.
justification: Table 3 and surrounding text give only percentage success rates with no counts, error bars, or setup details, confirming the omission.

weakness: Training/inference distribution mismatch (ground-truth trajectories/point clouds during training vs CLIPort/PointSAM estimates at inference) is not quantified with a controlled ablation.
justification: Section 3.3 describes this train/inference gap but Table 4 ablations do not include a ground-truth vs CLIPort-estimated input comparison, so the claim of missing quantification is accurate.

weakness: Ablation study does not test the unified codebook vs per-hand codebooks or cross-morphology distillation, which are the paper's claimed key novel contributions.
justification: Table 4 only ablates depth input, masked training, and physical refinement; no ablation of the codebook/distillation appears anywhere in the paper.

weakness: VQ-VAE diagnostic details are missing: codebook size K, dimension d_z, tokens per sequence, reconstruction accuracy, and codebook utilization are never reported.
justification: Section 3.2 defines K and d_z symbolically (Eq. 1) but never gives concrete values or reconstruction/utilization statistics anywhere in the text.

weakness: CLIPort-style vision module and Point-SAM are underspecified, without architecture details, training procedure, or independent accuracy evaluation.
justification: Section 3.3 references 'a CLIPort-style vision module' and PointSAM only briefly (Eq. 7-8) without further architectural or training detail or standalone evaluation.

weakness: The masking schedule p_t (linear, cosine, step-wise, etc.) is not specified, hindering reproducibility.
justification: Section 4.4 describes p_t increasing from 0 to 1 but never specifies its functional form, confirming the gap.

weakness: Query specification gap when integrated with observation-window methods: Algorithm 2 calls Algorithm 1 with a single Query State q, but Algorithm 1's integration point (line 8) does not specify what q is when the baselines accumulate attention over multiple queries (Algorithm 2 line 3: Ā = A.mean(dim=0)).
justification: The paper text (Algorithm 1's input list and Algorithm 2 lines 1-9) never specifies which query is passed to Algorithm 1 during the observation-window integration, leaving a genuine reproducibility gap.

weakness: Theory-algorithm connection is inspirational rather than derivational: the two-stage greedy Top-K algorithm is a heuristic inspired by the upper bound θ, not a formal minimization of it, and doesn't account for the (2-1/σ) weighting factor or entry interactions.
justification: Section 3.4 itself states 'directly minimizing the upper bound θ remains non-trivial,' confirming the algorithm is a heuristic approximation rather than an exact optimization, as the reviewer claims.

weakness: The α = 0.5 safeguard has an unanalyzed failure mode: Table 4 shows α=0.0 outperforms α=0.5 on Llama-3.1-8B (44.35 vs 43.77) but catastrophically underperforms on Mistral-7B (31.94 vs 42.85), and the paper doesn't explain why Mistral differs.
justification: The numbers match Table 4 in the paper exactly, and Section 4.5 only attributes the Mistral failure to 'a violation of the assumption for certain attention heads' without further explaining the model-specific cause.

weakness: No statistical uncertainty reported for Ruler results, which are based on only 100 samples per task, despite some large reported gains.
justification: Table 1 in the paper reports single point-estimate scores with no variance, standard error, or confidence interval, and the 100-samples-per-task setup is confirmed in Section 4.2.

weakness: Algorithm pseudocode inconsistency: Stage 1 (line 5) selects using plain attention weight A_i from Top_k of the product score 𝒜, while the prose describes Stage 1 as selecting by 'high attention weights' alone; also Algorithm 1 lists α=0.25 as input but experiments use α=0.5.
justification: The paper's Algorithm 1 box literally shows 'Hyper Parameter α = 0.25' while Section 4.1 states 'We set α = 0.5 in Algorithm 1 for all experiments,' and the notation mixing A_i and 𝒜 in lines 5 and 8 is indeed inconsistent with the Section 3.4 prose.

weakness: The H2O baseline is simulated (observing only the last 256 tokens) rather than run in its original form.
justification: Section 4.1 confirms: 'Since it requires global attention weights—unsupported by FlashAttention-2—it triggers OOM... we simulate H2O by observing the last 256 tokens' attention weights,' so this is a genuine (if disclosed) limitation of the H2O comparison.

weakness: Efficiency (TTFT/decoding latency) is reported only for SnapKV, not measured explicitly for AdaKV or HeadKV.
justification: Section 4.6 gives concrete TTFT and decoding latency numbers only for SnapKV and merely asserts (without data) that 'all cache eviction methods demonstrate same efficiency,' so the AdaKV/HeadKV overhead claim is unverified by reported numbers.

weakness: The Bayesian optimization framing does not reflect the actual implementation — no GP, no posterior, no uncertainty calibration, UCB weights all set to 1.
justification: Paper text confirms surrogate model is an LLM producing integer scores 0-100, and w_u=w_q=κ=1 with no tuning; this matches the review's claim exactly.

weakness: The 'three years of human research in two weeks' comparison (Figure 1/abstract) conflates incomparable quantities (multiple research groups over years vs. one well-resourced system for two weeks).
justification: The paper's Figure 1 does plot multiple independently published human methods across years against a single system's 15-day run with 16 H800 GPUs and no adjustment for compute/team differences, supporting the critique.

weakness: Missing error bars/variance on all main experimental results in Table 1, especially problematic for the small 1.9% LLM Inference Acceleration improvement.
justification: Table 1 in the paper reports single point values (190.25 vs 193.90 tokens/second etc.) with no confidence intervals or multi-seed runs anywhere in the text.

weakness: The 183.7% improvement framing exploits a very weak baseline (16.67%->47.46% accuracy), foregrounded as relative % in abstract/intro.
justification: The abstract states 'surpassing... SOTA methods... by 183.7%...' without noting the low absolute baseline value, which is only visible in Table 1.

weakness: The scaling analysis (Figure 6) does not support the 'near-linear' claim given only 3 informative points (0,0,1,4,11) that could be superlinear, with no error bars.
justification: Paper's own Figure 6 table shows exactly 0,0,1,4,11 for 1,2,4,8,16 GPUs, and no error bars/variance are reported for this stochastic process, supporting the critique.

weakness: No component-level ablations isolating surrogate model scores, acquisition function weighting, or memory synchronization scheme.
justification: The paper only reports one ablation (selection vs random sampling in Section 4.3); no ablation of individual architectural components is described anywhere in the text.

weakness: The human evaluation does not clearly establish reviewer independence, and the cross-system comparison uses DeepScientist's curated best 5 papers against others' publicly available (possibly curated) papers, undermining the 60% acceptance rate comparison.
justification: The paper states the papers compared 'may be curated' (Table 2 note) and never discloses whether the three human program committee members are independent of the project, supporting the critique.

weakness: Headline 5.17x data efficiency claim depends on nested power-law extrapolations from very few data points (4 parameter counts for regularized asymptote, 4 K values for ensemble asymptote), with only run-to-run seed variance reported, not confidence intervals on fitted asymptote parameters themselves.
justification: The paper fits A_D, alpha_D, E_D from exactly four parameter counts (150M-1.4B) and reports only that 'asymptotes vary by at most 0.02 loss across 3 seeds' (footnote 2), which is run-to-run variance, not a confidence interval on the extrapolated asymptote itself, matching the reviewer's critique.

weakness: The ensemble member scaling extrapolation to K -> infinity is uncontrolled since it is fit from only K in {1,2,3,5}, a qualitatively narrow and small range, especially since K=1 is a different regime (no ensembling).
justification: The paper's Figure 4/5 fits power laws in K using K in {1,2,3,5} and extrapolates to K -> infinity for the asymptote (3.34/3.17), exactly as described; the paper itself notes the qualitative claim (K=3 beats regularized asymptote) is directly measured while the full asymptote is an extrapolation.

weakness: There is a scale gap between the motivating regime (trillions of tokens) and the experimental evidence (200M-1.6B tokens), and the data scaling laws used to argue the efficiency gains persist at scale are themselves fit from only 4 token budgets and extrapolated.
justification: Section 5 explicitly fits data scaling laws from four token counts (200M, 400M, 800M, 1.7B) and extrapolates; the paper's own Section 5.3 language ('preliminary analysis suggests...will not disappear') is hedged, supporting the reviewer's point that this is an extrapolation with limited data.

weakness: The joint scaling recipe used in the headline 5.17x figure relies on heuristic (not fully tuned) hyperparameters for the ensemble members (2x epochs, 0.5x weight decay), rather than a full hyperparameter search.
justification: The paper states directly: 'we cannot fully find locally optimal hyperparameters due to experimental constraints. Instead, we use the heuristic of taking the optimal regularized hyperparameters with 2x epochs and 0.5x weight decay,' confirming the reviewer's claim.

weakness: The downstream evaluation is narrow, covering only 3 benchmarks (PIQA, SciQ, ARC Easy), and the reported 9% improvement is relative to the best unregularized model rather than the best regularized single model, which should be clarified.
justification: Section 7 confirms only PIQA, SciQ, and ARC Easy are used, and states 'our best ensemble outperforming our best unregularized model by 9%', matching the reviewer's characterization exactly.

weakness: The paper does not account for the enormous actual compute cost (wall-clock/hardware) of the proposed recipes despite framing the setting as having no compute constraints.
justification: The paper explicitly frames its setting as 'no compute constraints' throughout but never quantifies or discusses the practical wall-clock/hardware cost of training e.g. 8-epoch 1.4B models or 5-member ensembles, so this omission is real.

weakness: Internal inconsistency in Table 1: GPT-4o No Opt value for ACE_med Depth 1 (dev) is 26.30, inconsistent with 12.68 (Depth 5 dev) and 13.33 (Depth 5 test) for the same model/dataset, and the reported +Δ values in that row do not match optimized_score - No_Opt for either candidate value.
justification: Paper text (lines 149, 154, 159, 164) confirms GPT-4o No Opt values of 12.68, 26.30, 12.68, 13.33 across rows, and the deltas in the 26.30 row (22.32-26.30=-3.98 vs reported +4.98; 27.54-26.30=1.24 vs reported +14.86) are indeed inconsistent.

weakness: DeepSeek-R1 is quantized to 2.5 bits while o1, GPT-4o, and GPT-4.5 run at full precision, creating an apples-to-oranges comparison, justified only by a blog-post citation about math/reasoning benchmarks rather than task-specific evidence.
justification: Paper explicitly states DeepSeek-R1 was quantized to 2.5 bits using UnSloth, citing degradation benchmarks at 1.58 bits from a non-peer-reviewed source (Daniel Han & team, 2023), with no EE-specific precision-controlled experiment.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance reported for the single F1/accuracy numbers in Table 1/Table 3, despite small training sets and MCTS stochasticity; Figure 4's confidence intervals are only shown qualitatively as shaded regions with no numerical values.
justification: Paper indeed reports only point estimates in Table 1/3, and Figure 4 caption/description mentions shaded confidence-interval regions without numeric values, confirming the gap.

weakness: Unclear whether the No Opt baselines use the same batch prompting technique as the optimized runs, so some of the reported optimization gain could stem from batch prompting rather than prompt content improvement.
justification: The paper states batch prompting is used 'when querying M_task for answer generation (Step 1 in Fig. 3)' and notes a performance gain from it, but does not specify whether the No Opt baseline uses the same batch setup, leaving this ambiguity as described.

weakness: Non-counterfactual comparison in Table 3 only against the base model, leaving a gap between the abstract's claim of 'best performance in both counterfactual and original contexts' and the evidence, since strongest fine-tuning baselines are absent.
justification: Table 3 caption and surrounding text (lines 168-179) only discuss CopyPasteLLM vs base model improvements on PubMedQA/ConFiQA non-counterfactual settings; no Context-DPO/Canoe/ParamMute comparison appears there, while the abstract claims best performance in both settings.

weakness: Twist and Causal hallucination metrics in Table 2 are not explained in the main text (what they measure, direction of better performance, computation).
justification: The paper only says the tournament 'diagnoses two major hallucination modes—Twist and Causal' (line 83) without defining scale or direction, matching the reviewer's claim that these numbers are uninterpretable from the main text.

weakness: The DPO preference data pipeline omits key details (filtering thresholds, judge model identity, no inter-annotator agreement) and the answer-stamping procedure is not ablated.
justification: The main text describes multi-criteria filtering and an Elo-style LLM-as-Judge tournament with a stamping procedure (lines 83) but does not name the judge model or report thresholds/agreement in the main text, and no ablation isolating stamping is presented in the reviewed sections.

weakness: Inconsistent baseline coverage across base models in Table 1 (5 baselines for Llama-3-8B, 3 for Mistral-7B-v0.2, only Attributed for Llama-3.1-8B).
justification: This is a factual observation about table composition; the paper text does not contradict or address this imbalance, making it a legitimate reliability concern.

weakness: Context-Parameter Copying Capturing's knowledge-source attribution is a coarse proxy (context tokens vs parametric tokens) whose limitations (shared tokens, position alignment across sequences) are not acknowledged.
justification: The algorithm as described (Section 3.3, Figures 3-4) labels tokens by simple appear-in-context vs context-free-preference criteria without discussing shared-token ambiguity or cross-sequence alignment issues, and no such caveat is present in the paper text.

weakness: Unverifiable headline improvement percentages (7.7% and 14.4% over prior state-of-the-art weighted-averaging models) cannot be reconciled with the numbers shown in Table 1.
justification: Table 1 only reports deltas relative to the text-only linear baseline (Antonello et al. 2024 semantic linear model), and the paper never explicitly presents the 'prior SOTA weighted averaging' model's numbers side-by-side, so a reader cannot verify the abstract's 7.7%/14.4% figures from the table alone.

weakness: Ambiguous PCA fitting procedure: unclear whether PCA on the response matrix was fit on training data only or on the full (train+test) dataset, raising a possible leakage concern.
justification: Section 2.3 (line 52) only says PCA was applied to the 'aggregate response matrix' without specifying train/test split, and the paper does not address this ambiguity elsewhere in the text provided.

weakness: The 'unusually large improvements' framing is unsupported in the main text and only deferred to Appendix N.2.
justification: Deferring supporting quantitative justification to an appendix while stating the claim in the main text is standard practice, and the paper explicitly cites Appendix N.2 for the comparison; this is not a genuine flaw in the paper's argument.

weakness: No hyperparameter details (learning rate, optimizer, batch size, epochs, regularization) are given in the main text for the MLP.
justification: The paper explicitly directs readers to Appendix B.5 for encoder architecture details ('see Appendix B.5'), so requiring these to be repeated in the main text is an excessive demand rather than a genuine omission.

weakness: RED-based clustering modularity differences (0.155 vs 0.145 vs 0.068) are small and not accompanied by a statistical test or confidence interval in the main text.
justification: The paper reports only point-estimate modularity values in Section 3.1.2/Figure 1 without any significance test for the difference, so the claim of 'superior' clustering is asserted without statistical support.

weakness: Some neurolinguistic theory interpretations (dual-stream model, Motor Theory, Convergence-Divergence Zone) exceed what the correlational variance-partitioning evidence can support, and the paper only caveats this for one case (embodied semantics) but not uniformly.
justification: Section 3.3.2 explicitly caveats the embodied-semantics interpretation (line 190: 'our current design cannot distinguish between these explanations') but makes similarly strong claims about Motor Theory and CDZ theory without the same caveat, confirming an inconsistency in how the correlational evidence is presented.

weakness: Table 1 reports point estimates without error bars, confidence intervals, or significance markers, making it hard to assess reliability of close rankings (e.g., 4.10% vs 4.18% vs 4.29% r²).
justification: The main-text Table 1 indeed shows only single-number averages with significance testing relegated to Appendix C, so the main table itself lacks any indication of variance for the closely-spaced model comparisons.

weakness: Uncontrolled baseline comparison (naive MLP): asymmetric clipping thresholds and no matched compute budget between naive MLP and SCaSML
justification: The paper text confirms asymmetric clipping thresholds (e.g. LQG: 10 vs 0.1, DR: 10 vs 0.01) and Table 1 shows SCaSML runtime is consistently much higher than naive MLP without budget-matched comparison in the main text.

weakness: Missing uncertainty quantification for Monte Carlo results in Table 1 (no error bars/variance)
justification: Table 1 as shown reports single point estimates with no confidence intervals; the p-value significance test is only referenced as being in the appendix, not shown in main text.

weakness: Unsubstantiated claim that MLP error term E(M,N) is independent of the surrogate, when the modified nonlinearity F-tilde depends explicitly on the surrogate
justification: Eq. (7)/(121) explicitly defines F-tilde as depending on the surrogate û and its gradient, yet line 214 asserts E(M,N) is independent of the surrogate without justification in the visible text.

weakness: Heuristic convergence rate analysis conflates training points and Monte Carlo paths, treating cost as '2m function evaluations' despite vastly different per-evaluation costs
justification: Section 2.1 (lines 105-106) indeed uses this 2m-evaluation framing without accounting for the differing cost of a collocation point vs. simulating a full SDE trajectory, and Figure 4 plots error vs. collocation points, not wall-clock time.

weakness: The 'inference-time scaling' LLM analogy is a poor fit for SCaSML's computational profile
