justification: The paper's own Table 1 shows SCaSML taking far more runtime than the surrogate (e.g. 10-200x), which the review correctly notes departs from the LLM inference-time-scaling analogy of allocating the same model more compute tokens.

weakness: The abstract's '20-80%' improvement claim is broader than what DR results (6.6-10.9%) support
justification: The paper explicitly reports DR improvement of 6.6% to 10.9% (line 302), which is below the abstract's advertised 20-80% range, confirming the review's point.

weakness: 'Smaller PINN outperforming larger PINN' contribution claim has no supporting experiment in the main text
justification: This claim appears in the contributions list (line 33) but no corresponding experiment, figure, or table comparing surrogate sizes appears anywhere in the visible main text (Sections 3.1-3.4).

weakness: Novelty claims are somewhat oversold; defect correction for PDEs is classical and Fact 2.3's derivation is a direct algebraic manipulation
justification: The paper itself cites Bank & Weiser 1985 and Stetter 1978 as classical defect-correction references while still describing its derivation as 'the first derivation that preserves semi-linear structure' (line 31), supporting the review's more tempered framing of novelty.

weakness: The theoretical framework's Eq2 (that generation under an interpolated condition is a convex combination of vector fields at dataset conditions) does not logically follow from mere piecewise-linearity of the network; it would require linearity in the condition input over the relevant region, which is a stronger unproven claim, and Eq1 (the closed-form flow matching objective/training target) is attributed to the trained network without justification.
justification: The paper (Section 2.2, lines 45-57) presents Eq1 as the closed-form CFM vector field and then asserts Eq2 for interpolated conditions purely from the piecewise-linear hypothesis, without arguing that piecewise-linearity implies linearity in the condition variable specifically; this gap is real and unaddressed in the text.

weakness: The diversity metric (Eq8, average pairwise distance) and accuracy metric (Eq9, label MSE) are closely aligned with what Q_D and Q_A directly optimize for, and the paper provides no measure of physical plausibility/validity of generated shapes, only qualitative figures.
justification: Section 3.1 confirms the metrics are exactly average pairwise distance and label MSE, and no quantitative validity/plausibility metric appears anywhere in the paper text provided, only qualitative shape figures (Figs 3, 5, 6, 8).

weakness: The RBF label-prediction pipeline used by both Q_D and Q_A is underspecified -- no architecture, training procedure, hyperparameters, or prediction-accuracy evaluation is given.
justification: Lines 89 and 103 only mention 'we employ Radial Basis Function (RBF) Neural Networks' with no further architectural or training detail anywhere in the paper text provided.

weakness: No error bars, multiple random seeds, or statistical significance are reported across the active learning experiments.
justification: Section 3.2/Figure 4 description and surrounding text describe single curves per method with no mention of repeated runs or variance.

weakness: Key hyperparameters α, β, γ in Q_D (Eq4) and ω in Q_hybrid (Eq7) are introduced but never given concrete values or a sensitivity analysis.
justification: Eq4 and Eq7 define these coefficients symbolically; the paper text never states numeric values used in experiments, only that different ω values were compared in Fig7 without giving the actual tested numbers or a systematic sensitivity study.

weakness: The paper mislabels its diversity metric as a 'custom variant of the Vendi score' when it is simply average pairwise Euclidean distance, unrelated to the eigenvalue-based Vendi score formulation.
justification: Line 129 explicitly calls the average-pairwise-distance metric (Eq8) 'a custom variant of the Vendi score,' but the cited Vendi score (Friedman & Dieng 2022) is defined via kernel matrix eigenvalues, a materially different construction never connected to Eq8 in the text.

weakness: The paper does not report dataset/pool sizes or initial labeled set sizes, only stating that 6% of data is selected per iteration.
justification: Line 143 states '6% of the data is selected' per iteration but no total pool size or initial labeled set size is given anywhere in Sections 3.1-3.2.

weakness: Inconsistent spelling of an author's name across citations ('Scarvelis et al. (2023)' vs. 'Scardelis et al. (2023)').
justification: Line 23 uses 'Scarvelis et al. (2023)' while line 45 uses 'Scardelis et al. (2023)' referring to the same closed-form flow matching citation, confirming the inconsistency.

weakness: The Nemotron synergy experiment (Section 4.3.1) is confounded because Exp C uses 70% synthetic data (twice as much as Exp A/B's 35% each), so its superior performance may reflect volume rather than true synergy.
justification: The paper text confirms Exp A and B each replace 35% with one synthetic source while Exp C replaces 70% with an equal combination, so the comparison is not controlled for total synthetic volume.

weakness: No variance estimates or statistical significance are reported for any result (Table 2, Figure 3, Figure 4), making it unclear whether small gains (e.g., +0.26 avg at 134M) are real or within noise.
justification: The paper never mentions multiple seeds, error bars, or significance testing for any of its reported results.

weakness: The 'collecting more real data' baseline in Figure 3's entire-set experiment uses 195B unique tokens versus MGA's 250B unique tokens (50B real + 200B synthetic), so the claimed superior D-scaling may partly reflect more unique tokens rather than reformulation quality.
justification: The paper text confirms the 'collect more' baseline uses 195B via Full-FineWeb-Edu while MGA uses a 200B reformulation expansion of the original 50B data, an unequal comparison the paper does not address.

weakness: The validation loss paradox analysis in Section 4.3.3 lacks a calibration baseline (e.g., a known-collapsing model) to confirm the anomaly pattern is qualitatively distinct from actual model collapse, so the 'different learning strategy' interpretation remains speculative.
justification: The paper only compares real vs synthetic-trained models and does not run the same diagnostic on a model known to be undergoing collapse, leaving the interpretation unconfirmed as the reviewer notes.

weakness: The quality evaluation in Table 1 relies on self-scoring by the LLM itself, and the reported 'alignment rate of over 90%' from human cross-checking is underspecified (unclear tolerance, sample size, or inter-annotator agreement).
justification: The paper's own caption states outputs were 'scored on a 1-5 scale by the LLM itself' with only a vague mention of 'human-in-the-loop cross-checking, yielding an alignment rate of over 90%' with no further detail provided in the main text.

weakness: There is an unexplained parameter count discrepancy between the published SmolLM-360M (360M params) and the paper's reproduction 'SmolLM-360M (ours)' (377M params) in Table 2.
justification: Table 2 in the paper text shows exactly this discrepancy (360M vs 377M) with no explanation given anywhere in the visible main text.

weakness: The unconfoundedness constraint (Constraint 1) is theoretically vacuous — targets a quantity that is identically zero for any Z=g(X) in population regardless of instrument validity.
justification: The paper's own Lemma 1 and Section on Constraint 1 (lines 89-141) show Z is a deterministic function g(X); the reviewer's derivation showing Cov(Z, e_Y - E[e_Y|X,T])=0 trivially for any such Z is a valid mathematical critique the paper does not address.

weakness: Lemma 1's proof contains a mathematical error in the expansion of E[Z(e_Y - E[e_Y|X,T])].
justification: The paper states Lemma 1 (line 89) and its proof (lines 91-95); the reviewer correctly identifies that E[e_Y|X,T] is a random variable, not a constant, so it cannot be pulled out of the expectation as done in the paper's proof.

weakness: Covariance constraints are strictly weaker than the conditional independence conditions required for IV validity, and this gap is unaddressed; the MI variant is mentioned but not separately evaluated against the PC variant.
justification: Paper lines 99-103 and 131 define covariance-based constraints and mention an MI-based loss as an addition for non-linear settings, but no ablation or separate results comparing PC vs MI variants appear in the results/tables.

weakness: ATE evaluation (Table 1) is presented without variance estimates (standard errors/confidence intervals) despite using 50 bootstrap resamples, and results are mixed.
justification: Table 1's caption (line 380) confirms only bolded/italicized means and significance stars are reported, with no SE or CI shown, despite the underlying 50-bootstrap procedure that would allow it.

weakness: The paper contains strong overclaims, e.g., that ZNet solutions will always give a valid instrument representation since IV constraints are embedded in the loss, and that it works regardless of the unconfoundedness assumption.
justification: The abstract (line 9) and discussion (lines 393-394) make these claims, which are undermined by the vacuous Constraint 1 and the covariance/conditional-independence gap documented above.

weakness: The 'strategic task design' sweet-spot selection (asterisks in Fig. 5) is ad hoc/qualitative rather than a principled optimization, despite the paper claiming to enable 'principled, theory-driven experimental designs.'
justification: The paper's own text (line 151) says 'one might prioritize parameters that maximize posterior-coding discriminability while maintaining adequate likelihood-coding sensitivity' without defining a formal objective function, matching the review's claim exactly.

weakness: The posterior-coding information gap depends on an exact-matching condition (Eq. 4) between discretized observations, and the paper does not discuss how discretization resolution affects the gap or whether the matching condition holds meaningfully in continuous, finite-population settings.
justification: The paper discretizes observations and defines Eq. 4 as an exact equality condition (lines 79-81) but nowhere discusses discretization resolution effects, a genuine gap in the text.

weakness: The claim that maximizing information gap yields optimal experimental designs is validated only via simulation with known ground-truth coding, not through a predictive test on real data.
justification: Section 5's Allen dataset analysis is a consistency check (Δ^info≈0 for single-context uniform-prior data) rather than a forward test of the optimized multi-context design, as the paper itself frames it (lines 169-175).

weakness: The paper never addresses what magnitude of information gap constitutes a 'decisive' result for rejecting one hypothesis versus the other.
justification: The paper discusses convergence of decoder performance to the theoretical information gap (Fig. 3) but never translates gap magnitude into a decision rule or required effect size, a real omission.

weakness: The assumption that subjects adopt the intended context-specific prior (stated at line 59) is not stress-tested for sensitivity to partial or biased prior adoption in the main text.
justification: Line 59 states this assumption and line 196 only mentions imperfect priors as a future extension without quantifying sensitivity of the optimal designs to biased prior adoption, supporting the critique.

weakness: No comparison to any existing OAD method (LSTR, TeSTra, GateHub, IDN) on Ego-OAD, even in offline setting.
justification: The paper's tables only compare Pretrained Only, w/o COAD, and COAD (its own GRU model); no other prior OAD method is included as a baseline anywhere in the text.

weakness: The proposed training components (state continuity, orthogonal gradient, non-uniform loss) provide only modest gains over the simple continuous-training baseline while the abstract's 'up to 20%' framing conflates adaptation generally with the specific components.
justification: Table 1 shows COAD (26.0/76.0) vs w/o COAD (25.5/71.6) out-of-stream, a small gap, and COAD in-stream mAP (36.8) is lower than w/o COAD (39.0); Table 3 shows state continuity ablation changes mAP by only 0.1.

weakness: No efficiency measurements (FLOPs, memory, training overhead) despite motivating COAD by wearable hardware constraints.
justification: Sections 1 and 4.5 argue based on storage/compute constraints of wearable devices, but no such measurements appear anywhere in the experiments or tables.

weakness: The experimental split design (186 pretrain videos vs 1,177 in-stream) advantages the method by starting from a deliberately weak baseline.
justification: Section 5.1 confirms this split allocation and states it was chosen 'to better assess the impact of continuous learning,' but the paper does not test whether COAD's advantage persists with a stronger pretrained baseline.

weakness: EPIC-KITCHENS results receive insufficient analysis, e.g. w/o COAD crashing below Pretrained Only, and unexplained 10x gap in Pretrained Only Noun mAP between out-of-stream (31.4) and in-stream (3.8).
justification: Table 2 and the surrounding text confirm these numbers; the paper only vaguely attributes issues to 'fine-grained actions' without deeper analysis of the specific gap.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance reported across runs, especially concerning given some improvements are as small as 0.5 mAP.
justification: All reported results in Tables 1-4 are single point values with no error bars or multiple-run statistics.

weakness: No analysis of catastrophic forgetting despite continuous training on a stream without replay.
justification: The paper never measures performance on earlier vs later in-stream data or otherwise assesses forgetting; only aggregate in-stream/out-of-stream metrics are reported.

weakness: The 'label efficiency' claim for non-uniform loss (enabling training with sparse annotations) is unsupported since all experiments use dense annotations.
justification: Section 4.5 states the benefit is 'allowing training with sparse instead of dense frame-level annotations,' but no experiment in Section 5 actually trains with sparse labels to demonstrate this.

weakness: The orthogonal gradient projection is myopic, decorrelating only against the immediately preceding gradient g_{t-1}, missing longer temporal correlations; ablation shows the effect is modest.
justification: Eq. in Section 4.5 confirms the projection formula uses only g_{t-1}, and Table 3 shows removing it barely changes out-of-stream mAP (26.0 to 25.3).

weakness: TORCS comparison is asymmetric: β=0.5 (cautious reward) is used for the neural DRL policy while NDPS results in Table 1 are taken from the original β=1.0 setup in Verma et al. (2018), so the experiment does not control for training objective across representations; only 13/30 and 4/15 seeds successfully learned the training task under β=0.5, making it a selected subset.
justification: The paper itself states (line 209) that it changed β from 1.0 to 0.5 only for the neural policy while NDPS numbers in Table 1 come directly from Verma et al. (2018)'s original β=1.0 runs, and Table 1's caption confirms only 13/30 and 4/15 seeds learned the training task under β=0.5.

weakness: Abstract overstates PARKING results, claiming neural policies 'can match or exceed' programmatic ones across all three benchmarks, whereas the body reports mixed results for PARKING, and seed counts are asymmetric (30 PSM vs 15 DQN) without explanation.
justification: The abstract's blanket claim of matching/exceeding OOD generalization contradicts Section 4.3/4.4, which explicitly says PARKING results are mixed/ambiguous depending on the metric (lines 266-267, 274), and the seed asymmetry (30 vs 15, Table 3) is never justified in the text.

weakness: The FUNSEARCH proof-of-concept is too thin: no neural policy is trained on the same task to empirically demonstrate failure, key experimental details (maze topology, prompt structure, evaluation protocol) are missing from the main text, only three runs were performed, and FUNSEARCH's Python synthesis is less directly comparable to a bounded DSL like the KAREL grammar.
justification: Section 5's FUNSEARCH experiment (lines 304-308) indeed reports only three runs, no neural baseline on the SparseMaze task, and omits maze topology/prompt/evaluation details in the main text, matching the reviewer's specific claims.

weakness: HARVESTER remains essentially unsolved by 'PPO with a_{t-1}' (0.04 on 100x100), and the paper does not discuss why this task resists the approach while the other four KAREL tasks are solved perfectly.
justification: Table 2 confirms the 0.04 HARVESTER result, and the surrounding discussion in Section 4.2/4.4 discusses the MAZE wall-following success but never addresses the HARVESTER exception.

weakness: Uneven seed counts across comparisons (KAREL: 5 seeds for LEAPS/ConvNet/LSTM vs 30 for PPO with a_{t-1}; PARKING: 30 PSM vs 15 DQN; TORCS: 3 seeds NDPS vs 30/15 DRL) are not discussed by the paper as a potential confound.
justification: The seed-count numbers themselves are confirmed in the paper's table captions (Table 1, 2, 3), and no discussion of how these asymmetries might affect the validity of the comparisons appears in Sections 4 or 4.4.

weakness: Theorem 1.1 (nearest-prototype/Gaussian mixture bound) is analytically disconnected from the actual CaPT method, which uses deep networks with consistency regularization/pseudo-labeling, and the 2^(d/2) term makes the bound vacuous at pixel-level dimensionality without clarification of what feature space it applies to.
justification: The paper's theorem operates under a 'prototype-based Gaussian-mixture generative model' (Section 1) while the method described in Section 3 is a deep co-training/consistency-regularization pipeline; the paper never states the theorem's dimension d refers to a latent space rather than raw pixels, so the critique is well grounded in the text.

weakness: The comparison between CaPT and unimodal SSL baselines is in an asymmetric resource regime (CaPT uses an extra CLIP visual+text encoder), and the paper does not transparently discuss this capacity difference in the main text.
justification: The paper reports parameter/time/memory overhead in Table 4 but does not explicitly discuss in the main text whether gains stem from extra model capacity versus the co-training design; the ablation (Table 6) is not framed as addressing this specific concern.

weakness: The paper is missing a baseline using frozen CLIP zero-shot predictions as soft targets for the unimodal network's consistency loss, without co-training or adapter tuning.
justification: The paper's ablations (CaPT-Ada, CaPT-Deb, CaPT-Uni, only UPM, only MPM) do not include this exact simple distillation baseline, so this is a valid, checkable gap rather than an out-of-scope request since DebiasPL (the closest related work discussed) uses a different mechanism (pseudo-label injection into the labeled set, not soft-target distillation).

weakness: Standard deviations are reported for the USB benchmark (Table 1) but not for ImageNet (Table 2) or the one-label-per-class setting (Table 3), despite large claimed improvements.
justification: Tables 2 and 3 in the paper indeed show single point-estimate numbers with no ± values, unlike Table 1, confirming the reviewer's observation.

weakness: The entropy-based weighting (Eq. 11-12) is computed at the batch level, giving all samples in a batch the same module weight regardless of individual sample confidence.
justification: Equation 11 explicitly averages entropy over the batch (1/N sum_j) to produce a single H used for all samples' weights in Eq. 12, exactly as described.

weakness: The FGVCAircraft failure case is only briefly discussed in the conclusion and deferred to Appendix N rather than given a paragraph in the main experimental section.
justification: Section 4.4 mentions FGVCAircraft only in passing ('discussed in Appendix N') and the main discussion appears in the Conclusion section, confirming the reviewer's observation about placement.

weakness: Headline performance comparison (0.81 r-FID MMD VAR vs 0.92 r-FID vanilla VAR) is confounded by codebook size (K=8192 vs K=4096); at equal K=4096 the improvement is only 0.91 vs 0.92.
justification: Table 2/3 rows confirm MMD VAR at K=4096 gets 0.91 r-FID vs vanilla VAR K=4096 0.92, and the paper's abstract/Section 5 headline claim (line 125) touts the 0.81 vs 0.92 comparison without reporting vanilla VAR at K=8192.

weakness: Cross-dataset comparisons (Tables 8, 9, 10) are confounded because VQ-Transplant methods use a pretrained encoder-decoder while baselines are trained from scratch on the target dataset, with no controlled baseline where the original VQ module undergoes the same decoder-only adaptation.
justification: The paper's cross-dataset tables compare against baselines like RQVAE, VQGAN etc without an ablation isolating pretraining advantage from VQ-Transplant's contribution.

weakness: MMD-VQ shows no demonstrated advantage over Wasserstein VQ across Tables 3, 7, 8, 9, 10, undermining its claim as a distinct 'novel VQ method.'
justification: Table rows (e.g. 173-174, 178-179, 183-184, 188-189) show MMD and Wasserstein VAR results within 0.01-0.02 of each other and neither consistently dominates, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: Evaluation focuses solely on reconstruction fidelity, not downstream generation utility, despite the introduction motivating VQ tokenizers via their role in visual generation/vision-language modeling.
justification: The paper's evaluation metrics section (line 121) lists only reconstruction metrics (PSNR, SSIM, r-FID, LPIPS, r-IS); no downstream generative task evaluation is presented in the paper text reviewed.

weakness: Inconsistent metric direction for r-IS: Tables 2 and 3 mark r-IS with ↓ even though higher values are treated as better, while Table 7 correctly uses ↑ for the same metric.
justification: Line 135 and line 166/210 show r-IS labeled with ↓ while higher r-IS values (e.g., 201.0) are bolded as best, an internal inconsistency confirmed directly in the paper's table headers.

weakness: Framing mismatch: title/abstract promise to study likelihood inversion but experiments only measure relative AUROC performance via redefined Definition 3.3, never directly testing whether anomalies get higher likelihood than normal samples.
justification: The paper's Definition 3.3 (lines 73-77) is explicitly framed around AUROC comparison rather than direct likelihood comparison between normal and anomalous samples, and no experiment in the paper reports average log-likelihoods of normal vs anomalous samples for tabular datasets.

weakness: Hyperparameters were selected by optimizing average AUROC across all 47 datasets, leaking test-set information into model selection.
justification: The paper states verbatim: 'the hyperparameter combination with the highest average AUROC for all datasets is selected as the representative hyperparameter combination' (line 122), confirming this is exactly what was done without a held-out validation split.

weakness: Definition 3.3's thresholds β and γ are not specified with concrete values in the main text.
justification: The main text (lines 73-77, 124) uses β and γ symbolically and discusses cases informally ('the gap is very small,' 'cannot be judged') without ever stating numeric threshold values in the body text.

weakness: The IMDB failure case (AUROC=0.5013, near-random) is dismissed via Definition 3.3's thresholds rather than being analyzed for why the method fails.
justification: Line 124 confirms the paper dismisses imdb by noting the gap with the best comparison model is small and 'cannot be judged' as counterintuitive, without further investigating the near-random AUROC or providing likelihood/ID analysis specific to imdb.

weakness: Theorem 5.4 assumes independent features; the per-dimension contribution to the likelihood gap is not quantified for realistic tabular dimensions, weakening the theory's applicability to real non-independent data.
justification: The paper's own text (lines 164, 178) acknowledges independence is not guaranteed in raw data experiments and that Appendix D's theorem requires the independence assumption, supporting the reviewer's point about limited direct applicability.

weakness: Architecture-domain confound (NICE/MLP for tabular vs CNN-based flows like Glow/RealNVP for images) is acknowledged but no controlled experiment (e.g., NICE on CIFAR-10 vs SVHN) is run to separate architecture from domain effects.
justification: The paper discusses the MLP vs CNN distinction (lines 192, 232) citing Schirmeister et al. but does not report any experiment applying NICE/NF-SLT directly to CIFAR-10/SVHN to isolate the architecture effect from the domain effect.

weakness: Table 4 shows ID estimates for only 4 tabular datasets while Figure 1's right panel plots many more tabular points, and the paper does not clarify how many datasets were used or whether the 4 shown are representative.
justification: Line 224 confirms Table 4 reports MLE/TwoNN estimates for only MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, SVHN (4 image datasets) plus a limited tabular set, without explicit justification of representativeness relative to the broader ADBench set referenced elsewhere.

weakness: Missing control for uniform deepening - no experiment isolating whether gains come from dynamic selection vs. simply adding extra computation/capacity during SFT (no uniform-deepening baseline).
justification: The paper's ablations (Table 4) only vary routing/threshold control quality and selection ratio; there is no experiment applying the extra nested pass uniformly to all tokens, so this genuine gap is well-grounded.

weakness: No statistical reliability information (no seeds, std devs, or confidence intervals), and some 30B gains are within a plausible noise range (e.g., BBH +0.13, MATH +0.15).
justification: The paper indeed reports only single-run point estimates in Tables 1 and 2 with no variance/seed information, so this critique is supported by the text.

weakness: The nested pass truncates attention context (selected tokens only attend to each other, not the full original sequence), and the paper does not discuss this design trade-off or analyze its effect.
justification: Eq. 3 packs only selected tokens into a compact subsequence for the nested layer, and the paper never explicitly discusses or analyzes this attention-context limitation.

weakness: The ITT baseline is the only direct method comparison and is essentially ineffective, providing limited information; additional baselines would better contextualize DND's gains.
justification: Table 1 shows ITT yields near-zero average improvement (59.58 vs 59.53), and it is indeed the only directly compared prior method in the main results, supporting the critique.

weakness: Parameter capacity confound: AIR's improvement may partly stem from having more IH-dedicated parameters (30-50x more than baselines) rather than per-layer injection, and no ablation isolates this.
justification: The paper reports 0.4M params for AIR (Sec 4 Overheads) vs 12K for ISE and 8K for Delimiters but does not include any parameter-matched ablation to isolate capacity from per-layer distribution effects.

weakness: Gradient-based attacks (GCG) are evaluated at a fixed step budget (50/200) without convergence analysis, so it's unclear if AIR hardens the model or merely raises attack cost; Figure 7 curves for AIR appear still decreasing at the final step.
justification: The paper (Sec 5.4, Fig 7) only runs GCG for 50 or 200 steps and states loss 'diminishes with more GCG optimization steps' without reporting convergence or justifying the different step budgets for SFT vs DPO.

weakness: Overstated reduction range: the claimed 1.6x-9.2x reduction is inconsistent with Table 1, where the minimum ratio (Llama-3.1-8B DPO GCG: ISE=4.0, AIR=2.8) is ~1.43x, below the stated 1.6x floor.
justification: Table 1 shows ISE=4 and AIR=2.8 for Llama-3.1-8B DPO GCG, giving 4/2.8≈1.43, which is below the abstract/conclusion's stated 1.6x lower bound.

weakness: Underspecified inference-time determination of privilege levels (k_i): the paper does not explicitly state how k_i is assigned to tokens at inference time.
justification: The paper describes privilege levels via segment definitions (Sec 5.3, Fig 5) during training but does not explicitly detail the inference-time procedure for assigning k_i to arbitrary input tokens, though it can be inferred from segment structure.

weakness: Factually incorrect claim about adaCR in the ablation section: paper states AdaSVD already outperforms SVD-LLM without adaCR, but Table 3b shows AdaSVD-Const at 50% (27.33) is worse than SVD-LLM (27.19).
justification: Verified against Table 3b: at 50% compression, AdaSVD Const CR = 27.33 vs SVD-LLM = 27.19, contradicting the blanket claim in Section 4.3 that 'AdaSVD already outperforms SVD-LLM without using adaCR.'

weakness: Ablation reveals non-trivial component interactions (neither adaComp alone nor adaCR alone reliably beats SVD-LLM at 50%, but combined they do) that the paper does not explain or acknowledge.
justification: Confirmed from Table 3a/3b at 50%: AdaSVD w/o adaComp = 30.00 (worse than SVD-LLM 27.19), AdaSVD w/o adaCR = 27.33 (worse than SVD-LLM), yet full AdaSVD = 25.58; the paper's text in Section 4.3 does not discuss this interaction.

weakness: The adaCR importance metric (cosine similarity between layer input and output) is not theoretically justified and is not compared against alternative importance measures.
justification: Section 3.2 introduces the cosine-similarity importance metric with no theoretical justification or comparison to alternative importance measures (e.g., gradient/Fisher-based, output norm), matching the paper's actual content.

weakness: The minimum retention ratio (mrr) and iteration count k used for the main results in Table 1 are not disclosed; these hyperparameters are only varied in ablations (Table 3c/3d).
justification: Table 1 and the surrounding text (Section 4.1/4.2) do not state which mrr or iteration count values were used to produce the main results, only the ablation tables 3c and 3d vary these parameters.

weakness: No variance or confidence intervals are reported despite calibration data being randomly sampled (256 samples from WikiText-2), which is relevant given some method gaps are narrow (e.g., 27.19 vs 27.33 at 50%).
justification: The Implementation Details paragraph states calibration data is randomly selected but no repeated trials, standard deviations, or confidence intervals appear anywhere in the paper text provided.

weakness: Mismatch between claimed DP guarantees and what is actually delivered: paper repeatedly claims to 'provide differential privacy' / 'strong privacy guarantees' but only computes empirical RD on test-set pairs without a formal worst-case bound derived from mechanism design, and without a specific adjacency notion.
justification: The paper's Definition 2.2 requires a bound for any pair of adjacent inputs, but Section 3.2 explicitly states 'We do not assume any specific notion of adjacency between examples' and reports empirical max RD over test-set pairs, not a derived formal bound; yet the abstract and conclusion use language like 'strong privacy guarantees.'

weakness: No comparison against established differentially private methods such as DP-SGD; only compared to vanilla BERT, dropout+weight decay, and a VIB ablation (VTDP).
justification: The Baselines section (Section 4) only lists Base, +REG (dropout/weight decay), and the VTDP ablation; no DP-SGD or other formal-DP baseline is described anywhere in the paper.

weakness: No ex-ante privacy budget control: noise is controlled by hyperparameters λ_D and λ_G with no known mapping to a privacy budget, so practitioners cannot specify a target ε in advance; BDP/RD values are computed ex-post on the test set.
justification: Equation 5 shows λ_D, λ_G as regularization weights, and Section 4.1 confirms BDP/RD are reported post-hoc from 'full results for all regularization strengths' rather than derived from a target ε chosen beforehand.

weakness: Experimental protocol selects the best-performing run out of five, so reported privacy-utility numbers are conditioned on favorable runs and stability across runs cannot be assessed from the main text.
justification: Section 4.1 states 'we perform five independent runs and select the best-performing run on the validation set for final evaluation,' and no mean/std across runs appears in the visible paper text.

weakness: Overclaimed consistency: paper says NVDP 'consistently occupies the most favorable region of the plot' but on QQP NVDP has worse RD than VTDP (1.14 vs 0.85) despite higher accuracy, and on SST-2 VTDP has higher accuracy with identical BDP.
justification: Table 1 confirms QQP: NVDP RD 1.14 vs VTDP RD 0.85 (worse), and SST-2: VTDP accuracy 92.3 vs NVDP 91.7 with identical BDP 10.90, directly contradicting the unqualified 'consistently' claim in Section 4.2.

weakness: BDP values (ε_μ = 10.70-22.20) are called 'strong privacy' without calibration to standard DP norms, which could mislead readers about what these numbers mean.
justification: The paper indeed uses 'strong privacy guarantees' (abstract) and 'strong, practical privacy budgets' (conclusion) for ε_μ values of 10-22 without any discussion relating these to standard DP epsilon conventions.

weakness: The choice of λ = 1.1 for RDP is very close to 1, approximating KL divergence which is poorly suited for DP; the choice of λ should be justified and its sensitivity analyzed.
justification: Section 4.1 states 'we fix the Rényi order to λ = 1.1' without justification or sensitivity analysis in the visible text, and the paper itself notes λ near its lowest value reduces to KL-divergence (Section 2.1).

weakness: Training data and experimental controls not fully disclosed for the key Qwen-Image experiments (RCGM baseline vs TWINFLOW), making it unclear whether the large GenEval gap on Qwen-Image-20B is attributable to method vs. data/preprocessing differences.
justification: The paper never states whether Qwen-Image-RCGM baseline was trained on identical data/schedule as TWINFLOW; only Fig. 4b is explicitly captioned 'trained on the same dataset', and the paper itself attributes SANA-Sprint's DPG-Bench edge to 'extensive, proprietary training data' (line 332), showing data differences are a live confound the paper doesn't rule out elsewhere.

weakness: The KL-to-rectification-loss derivation uses a stop-gradient heuristic presented as though it follows from the KL gradient, but the gradient of Eq. (9) does not actually match Eq. (6) since the stop-gradient removes the theta-dependence of Delta_v.
justification: Eq. (9) explicitly applies sg[.] to Delta_v, and the text at line 151 says this is done 'to construct a tractable loss that produces this gradient structure' without acknowledging that this breaks the exact correspondence to (6), supporting the reviewer's point.

weakness: The "self-adversarial" label used throughout the paper is imprecise since the method is a velocity-field consistency regularizer, not a true minimax adversarial objective.
justification: The method as described in Sec 3.1-3.2 minimizes a difference between two velocity fields produced by the same network with no opposing discriminator/generator or saddle-point optimization, so the repeated 'self-adversarial' framing (Sec 3.1 heading, lines 43,105,109,163) is a legitimate labeling concern.

weakness: The paper criticizes Qwen-Image-Lightning for mode collapse but provides no quantitative diversity metric (e.g., LPIPS variance, recall) for TWINFLOW itself to substantiate its own claim of avoiding mode collapse.
justification: Table 3 and line 311 only describe mode collapse qualitatively/via near-identical GenEval-DPG outputs for other baselines; no quantitative diversity metric for TWINFLOW appears anywhere in the provided text.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance reporting for benchmark numbers in Tables 2-4; all are single-point estimates.
justification: Tables 2-4 report single numeric GenEval/DPG-Bench/WISE scores with no standard deviation or confidence interval columns anywhere in the paper text provided.

weakness: The abstract's claim that ICW is a 'model-agnostic' approach is unsupported since the paper only tests two OpenAI models (GPT-4o-mini, GPT-o3-mini) and detection performance varies drastically between them.
justification: The paper (Section 5.1) confirms only gpt-4o-mini and gpt-o3-mini were tested, both proprietary OpenAI models, and Table 2 shows Initials/Acrostics ICW near chance (AUC ~0.57-0.62) on GPT-4o-mini vs near-perfect on GPT-o3-mini, directly undercutting a model-agnostic claim.

weakness: The IPI setting experiments have no baselines to compare against, since PostMark and YCZ+23 are inapplicable there.
justification: Table 2 shows dashes for baselines in the IPI columns, and the paper itself states 'These baselines are not applicable in the IPI setting,' confirming no comparative baseline was used to calibrate IPI detection results.

weakness: No confidence intervals or variance reporting are given for AUC, T@1%F, T@10%F, or LLM-as-a-Judge scores across the 500 watermarked/500 human text evaluations.
justification: Section 5.1 and Tables 2-3 report only point estimates with no mention of bootstrapping, multiple seeds, or confidence intervals anywhere in the text.

weakness: LLM-as-a-Judge evaluation shows a systematic bias favoring LLM-generated text (unwatermarked GPT-o3-mini scores 4.99/5 vs human 4.24/5), confounding the text quality comparisons.
justification: Table 3 confirms Unwatermarked scores of 4.982/5.000/4.994 versus Human scores of 4.318/4.440/3.946, and the paper offers no human evaluation to cross-check this gap.

weakness: The IPI threat model's assumptions (full-PDF upload, no preprocessing that strips hidden text, single-turn interaction, unedited output) remain largely untested, making the IPI results a proof-of-concept rather than a demonstrated practical defense.
justification: The paper itself acknowledges 'a detailed investigation of attack and defense methods is left for future work' (Section 3.2), confirming these assumptions were not stress-tested.

weakness: Lexical ICW shows notably lower robustness than baselines under word replacement (AUC 0.758) and deletion (AUC 0.857) attacks, indicating a practical evasion vulnerability.
justification: Figure 3 data reported in the paper explicitly lists Lexical AUC of 0.758 (replacement) and 0.857 (deletion), both below the YCZ+23 and PostMark baselines shown in the same figure.

weakness: The contribution of auxiliary policies M versus the group-relative objective is not disentangled; no ablation trains GoalRank without M.
justification: Section 3.3 explicitly constructs groups B_u by combining generator output with auxiliary policy outputs, but no ablation removing M and using only generator-sampled lists is reported in the paper.

weakness: The gap between offline improvements (~17-25%) and online improvements (~0.1-1.2%) is large and unaddressed by the paper.
justification: Table 1 and Table 4 show this discrepancy and the paper (Section 4.2.3, Conclusion) never discusses or explains the magnitude difference.

weakness: Theorem 1 and the training objective (Equation 5) are narratively linked but formally disconnected; the claim 'we showed theoretically that GoalRank admits scaling laws' (line 274) overstates the connection since Theorem 1 is an existence result about generator-only function classes, not about the group-relative trained policy.
justification: Theorem 1 (Section 3.1) concerns existence of a large generator-only model with lower approximation error, independent of the group-relative training procedure introduced later in Section 3.2, so the line 274 framing is an overstatement.

weakness: The group-relative normalization in Equation 4 (z-score normalization) is justified only heuristically and not formally derived from the evidence bound.
justification: The paper derives the evidence bound (lines 134-140) and then introduces the biased reward and Equation 3/4 as a practical construction under the order-preservation condition, without a formal derivation showing Equation 4 follows necessarily from the bound.

weakness: The HTE learning extension (Section 5) lacks theoretical grounding for why pairwise averaging of outcome regression models produces a strong HTE estimator, and the ablation study (Table 5) varies only loss components while keeping the aggregation strategy fixed, conflating the effect of novel losses with the effect of aggregation.
justification: The paper itself only offers 'Surprisingly, our experiments show that this estimator performs exceptionally well' (line 228) with no theoretical justification, and the conclusion admits 'A remaining limitation is our use of a simple uniform averaging scheme,' confirming the gap; Table 5's ablation indeed only toggles L_ce/L_const, never testing aggregation with standard Dragonnet/TARNet losses.

weakness: The asymptotic theory (Theorem 1) assumes Φ(X) is fixed/known, but in the implemented method Φ(X) is adaptively learned from data via the neural network, creating a gap between the formal guarantees and the actual procedure run.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'Φ(X) is a representation of X adaptively learned from data' (line 110) while Theorem 1's correct-specification condition is stated in terms of a fixed working model, and the paper only partially addresses this via a sensitivity analysis in Appendix F.3 rather than incorporating representation-learning uncertainty into the theory.

weakness: The paper frames avoiding sample splitting as an advantage but does not discuss the potential overfitting/bias trade-offs that cross-fitting (used in Gao 2025) is designed to guard against.
justification: The paper states 'our proposed methodology does not require sample splitting' and 'The key derivation ... are conducted using the full dataset without sample splitting' (Section 4.4) but nowhere discusses the risk this poses relative to Gao's cross-fitting approach, matching the reviewer's claim of a missing discussion.

weakness: Standard deviations in Table 1 are large relative to the reported performance differences (e.g., IHDP √e_PEHE^in: 0.638±0.138 vs DCFR 0.741±0.068), and no paired significance test is reported to establish reliability of the improvements.
justification: Table 1 in the paper indeed reports these exact values with substantial standard deviations, and no paired significance test or confidence interval comparison for Table 1 results appears anywhere in the visible paper text.

weakness: Data-attribution claim (contribution i, Corollary 1's 'fewest examples') is asserted with 'see Section 7' but Section 7 contains no such experiment (no top-weighted examples table, no ablation).
justification: Section 7 (7.1-7.4) only covers detoxification, first-order equivalence check, layer-depth gamma, and spectral optimality on ImageNet — no experiment validates the data-attribution/provenance claim referenced at line 130.

weakness: The practical workflow (contribution iv: 'steer first, trace provenance, edit weights only when the geometry demands it') is never tested end-to-end.
justification: No experiment in Section 7 demonstrates the full steer-trace-edit workflow; only isolated pieces (steering, gamma diagnostic) are tested separately.

weakness: The slope of 1.50 in Figure 1's linearity experiment is unexplained/undiscussed despite being inconsistent with a true linear regime.
justification: The paper states only 'consistent with the expected linear regime' (line 239) without any discussion of why slope=1.5 rather than 1.0, or attempts to explain via damping/Gauss-Newton/perturbation size.

weakness: IAS underperforms CAA baseline in Table 1 (higher toxicity and perplexity) without discussion, and lacks comparison to random directions or other baselines.
justification: Table 1 shows IAS worse than CAA on both metrics (0.0164 vs 0.0150 toxicity, 13701 vs 13291 PPL) and the text (Section 7.1) presents the numbers with no commentary on this result, and no random-direction or additional baseline comparison appears anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The spectral optimality experiment (Figure 3) lacks methodological detail: number of random directions sampled, p-value computation method, whether the class was pre-registered.
justification: Section 7.4 only states p=0.00498, z=3.55 for one ImageNet class without specifying sample count or p-value methodology.

weakness: Experiments are limited to GPT-2 Medium and ResNet-50, but the paper claims tools 'scale to billion-parameter models' without validating on any modern large model.
justification: Line 25 claims scaling to billion-parameter models, yet Section 7 setup states experiments use only GPT-2 Medium (354M) and ResNet-50, no larger LLM is tested.

weakness: Table 1 reports point estimates for toxicity/perplexity without variance or confidence intervals despite stochastic sampling over 500 TOXIGEN prompts.
justification: Table 1 lists single mean values with no error bars, std, or CI reported anywhere in Section 7.1.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance reported for any result; single-seed point estimates throughout.
justification: The paper's tables report single average@16 numbers with no confidence intervals, standard errors, or multiple-seed runs mentioned anywhere in the experimental setup.

weakness: HES model-dependence is under-characterized relative to the 'intrinsic' claim; cross-checkpoint stability and cross-family transfer not tested, and default scoring model not explicitly stated.
justification: The paper only demonstrates same-family cross-size transfer (Qwen3-0.6B to Qwen3-8B) and does not test cross-checkpoint stability or cross-family transfer, nor explicitly state which model provides probabilities in the default setting.

weakness: The Length baseline is surprisingly competitive and the cost-benefit trade-off between HES and Length is not discussed despite the paper claiming a 'clear advantage'.
justification: Table 1/5 numbers cited (31.14 vs 30.67, and cases where Length outperforms HES) are drawn from the paper's own tables, and the paper does not include an explicit compute cost-benefit discussion.

weakness: Sensitivity analysis reveals domain-dependence (flat curves for MMLU STEM and LiveCodeBench) that goes unremarked/undiscussed.
justification: The reviewer accurately notes that the paper presents the sensitivity results as supporting robustness without discussing why some benchmarks show flat/insensitive curves.

weakness: RL improvement from Pos-High/Neg-Rand is concentrated on a single benchmark (HMMT24) with regressions elsewhere, unremarked in the paper.
justification: The per-benchmark breakdown shows uneven gains/regressions that the paper reports but does not discuss in terms of variance across benchmarks.

weakness: The Forking-Only baseline achieves nearly identical performance to Full-Dataset despite using a different mechanism, and this is not discussed to clarify what HES adds.
justification: This comparison of numbers exists in the paper's tables but the paper does not explicitly discuss the implication for what data-selection contributes beyond gradient masking on forking tokens.

weakness: The 'quality' framing slides between correctness and complexity/informativeness inconsistently, since incorrect RL responses have higher HES than correct ones.
justification: Figure 1 shows incorrect responses have higher HES (0.68) than correct (0.29), which is in tension with using HES to select 'high-quality' data elsewhere, a genuine conceptual imprecision the paper doesn't clarify.

weakness: The paper does not explicitly state which model provides the probability distributions for HES computation in the default (non-transfer) setting.
justification: This is a genuine specification gap; the paper's HES definition and experimental setup do not explicitly name the scoring model for the default configuration, only implying it via table structure.

weakness: Obs. 2 overgeneralizes that GraphRAG excels in complex tasks, but on the Medical dataset RAG with reranking outperforms or matches every GraphRAG method on Complex Reasoning, Contextual Summarize, and Fact Retrieval; this negative pattern is not discussed in the observations or conclusion.
justification: Obs.2 (line 227) states a blanket claim without qualification, and the paper's own observations (Obs.4-6) never engage with why the Medical dataset's dense structure fails to produce the same GraphRAG advantage seen on Novel, confirming the gap the reviewer identifies.

weakness: The paper's interpretive claims conflate 'graph structure' with full-system pipeline differences, attributing performance gains to graph structure without isolating its marginal contribution from other pipeline differences (entity extraction, retrieval mechanism, etc.).
justification: The paper frames its central question as understanding graph structure's role (Q3, abstract) but only compares complete GraphRAG vs RAG pipelines (Table 3/4) without an ablation isolating graph traversal from other components, which the paper itself lists as a nice-to-have improvement.

weakness: The Context Relevance metric (semantic similarity between question and retrieved context) may structurally penalize GraphRAG methods that retrieve broader, multi-topic community summaries, and the paper doesn't address whether the metric itself is biased.
justification: The paper defines Context Relevance as semantic alignment (line 233) and attributes low scores to 'excessive token accumulation'/'redundant information' (Obs.9) rather than considering the metric's inherent bias toward narrow retrieval, matching the reviewer's specific, verifiable concern.

weakness: No variance or statistical significance is reported for any result in Tables 3 and 4, making it hard to assess whether close comparisons are meaningful.
justification: Scanning the paper text, all results are presented as single point estimates with no mention of standard deviations, multiple runs, or significance tests.

weakness: Basic dataset statistics (questions per task level, corpus size, inter-annotator agreement) are missing from the main text.
justification: The paper defers such details to Appendix C/E (line 132) and the visible main text does not report question counts, corpus token/document counts, or IAA figures.

weakness: The question generation process is underspecified -- unclear whether questions were human-written, LLM-generated, or bootstrapped, and what quality controls beyond 'rigorous validation and refinement' were applied.
justification: Lines 130-132 describe question generation only abstractly ('calibrate questions by progressively integrating evidence types') without stating the generation method or concrete QA process, deferring to an appendix not in the provided text.

weakness: The 'Efficiency' axis in the Figure 4 radar charts is not defined, despite token costs being reported separately in Section 4.4.
justification: The Figure 4 caption (line 191-193) lists Efficiency as one of four radar axes but the paper never explains how it is computed or how it relates to the token-cost tables (Table 6/7) presented later in Section 4.4.

weakness: Table 3 uses 'ES' and 'Cov' columns for Creative Generation without a directly labeled 'Faithfulness' column, inconsistent with the text stating faithfulness is the metric used for that task.
justification: Line 187 states faithfulness is used for Type 4 (creative generation) questions, while Obs.3 (line 229) separately references 'evidence coverage' for the novel dataset, indicating an inconsistency in how the metric is labeled/reported that matches the reviewer's observation.

weakness: The hybrid distribution q_e/q_c that underlies the consistency condition and Γ_k(t) is underspecified — the paper only describes it informally as a 'hybrid distribution that treats the learner's predictions as targets while borrowing components from the environment as needed' (§3.2), without a formal definition, leaving readers unable to determine how to instantiate it in specific domains.
justification: The paper text confirms this exact informal, non-operational description in §3.2 and never gives a formal construction for supervised learning, RL, or generative modelling.

weakness: The paper claims its definition 'disentangles forgetting from backward transfer' but never empirically tests this against existing CL forgetting metrics (e.g., backward transfer, average accuracy drop) in a setting where they diverge.
justification: The experiments in §5.1-5.4 only show properties of Γ in isolation; there is no head-to-head comparison with conventional CL metrics anywhere in the paper text.

weakness: The RL experiment is too thin (a single DQN agent on Cartpole with 10 seeds, §5.4/Figure 5) to support the sweeping claim that 'forgetting is an essential component of RL.'
justification: The paper text confirms only one environment (Cartpole) and one algorithm (DQN) are used, yet §5.4 makes the broad claim 'demonstrating that forgetting is an essential component of RL.'

weakness: There is a gap between the theoretical definition of Γ_k(t) as a divergence over distributions of infinite future sequences (Definition 4.6, H^{t+k:∞}) and the empirical computation, which appears to use KL/MMD on single predicted outputs, without the main text explaining how the infinite-dimensional distributions are marginalized or approximated.
justification: The paper text for Figure 3 explicitly defers to 'See [SF] for details on the experimental implementation' rather than explaining the bridge in the main text, confirming the gap.

weakness: The forgetting-efficiency trade-off analysis in §5.3 is correlational and confounded, since varying SGD momentum or model size changes multiple aspects of learning dynamics simultaneously, so the causal interpretation ('effective approximate learners utilise forgetting as a mechanism') is not well supported by the experimental design.
justification: The paper text shows §5.3 only varies momentum and parameter count and observes correlation with Γ, then asserts the causal-sounding claim without controls isolating forgetting.

weakness: There is a notation inconsistency between q_c (used in Definition 4.5, line 215) and q_e (used in §3.2/§4.2), which is never reconciled or explained as referring to the same or different distributions.
justification: The paper text confirms Definition 4.5 uses q_c while §3.2 and the surrounding text (e.g. line 201, 203) use q_e, with no explanation connecting the two symbols.

weakness: Minor spelling inconsistency: 'backward transfer' is used in some places (e.g. lines 15, 165, 307) while 'backwards transfer' is used elsewhere (line 41).
justification: The paper text confirms both 'backwards transfer' (§2, Related Work) and 'backward transfer' (Introduction, Conclusion) are used inconsistently.

weakness: No variance or error bars on any throughput measurement across Figures 8-10; single-point measurements make it hard to distinguish real improvement from run-to-run noise, especially for the RL 'up to 10%' speedup.
justification: The paper reports all throughput numbers (Figures 8, 9, 10) as single point values with no mention of repeated runs, seeds, or variance/error bars anywhere in the text.

weakness: Inconsistency between the text, which states LB-Mini 'applies only to ODC' (Section 5.1), and Figure 8's legend, which lists 'Collective LB-Mini' as one of the compared methods.
justification: Paper text (line 179) says 'As LB-Mini can produce different number of microbatches for different devices, it applies only to ODC,' yet the Figure 8 caption explicitly lists 'Collective LB-Mini (purple triangles)' as a compared method, a direct contradiction.

weakness: Figure 9's y-axis is labeled 'Samples per Second' without noting that RL measurements only record training time and exclude rollout, which could mislead readers about end-to-end throughput.
justification: The paper states 'we only record the model training time in RL, ignoring forward-only parts like actor rollout' (Section 5.1) but Figure 9's axis and caption do not carry this caveat, matching the reviewer's claim.

weakness: The '50% idle time' motivational claim in the introduction is not backed by any concrete evidence in the main text and is deferred entirely to Table 6 in the appendix.
justification: Section 1 states 'workload imbalance can still result in device idle times of up to 50% during long-sequence supervised fine-tuning (see Table 6)' with no supporting numbers or configuration given in the main body.

weakness: LB-Micro is only vaguely described as 'a heuristic-based packing baseline' without specifying the heuristic, deferring details entirely to Appendix C.
justification: Section 5.1 describes LB-Micro only as 'a heuristic-based packing baseline designed to minimize workload imbalance across devices within the same microbatch,' with no further detail in the main text, confirming the omission.

weakness: Garbled equation at Section 2, lines 137-139: the derivation writes L_{||·||_ℋ}(f) on both sides of an inequality (should distinguish H from ℋ), making the derivation confusing even though Proposition 2.5 states the correct result.
justification: Confirmed by reading lines 137-139 of the paper: both sides of the displayed inequality and the following line use identical notation L_{||·||_ℋ}(f), which is indeed confusing/garbled as the review describes, even though the final Proposition 2.5 is stated correctly.

weakness: Misleading framing of the Õ(T^{-1/4}) claim in the contributions bullet (Section 1, line 40): it references theorems that are actually in Appendix D (stochastic setting) while the main-text Section 3 theorems give Õ(T^{-1/2}) rates for the deterministic setting.
justification: Line 40 explicitly cites 'Theorems D.2, D.7 and D.8' for the T^{-1/4} rate, and the main-text Theorems 3.1/3.2 (lines 164-182) are stated for the deterministic setting with different rate, confirming the review's claim of a main-text/appendix mismatch.

weakness: Slight overstatement in Section 3 (line 182) that adaptive smoothness Λ_ℋ(f) alone 'governs' the convergence rate, when the bound also depends logarithmically on ‖S_T‖_op via gradient norms.
justification: Line 182 confirms the text states the Λ_ℋ(f) 'governs the convergence rate' with an additional log d factor and (per Theorem 3.1 discussion) dependence through ‖S_T‖_op, supporting the review's nuance that the statement is a slight simplification.

weakness: Assumption 1 (independence of origination decisions across borrowers) is stated without defense or sensitivity analysis, and could overstate precision if it fails.
justification: The paper only states in text that the assumptions 'do not appear very strong to us' (p.138) without empirical justification or robustness analysis under dependence, matching the review's critique.

weakness: The restriction to size-2 clusters substantially limits generality and is under-analyzed, and the paper does not report how many larger clusters are discarded.
justification: Footnote 4 confirms all results are based on size-2 clusters, and the paper provides no count/discussion of discarded larger clusters.

weakness: The recall bound is relative, not absolute, and the abstract's phrasing could mislead readers about the 92% recall figure applying to real data.
justification: Corollary 1 shows P_tot is unobservable in the real application, yet the abstract states 'minimal loss in relative recall' without flagging that the concrete 92% figure (Section 3) is simulation-only.

weakness: No comparison against any baseline method for detecting cross-applicants.
justification: The paper's methodology and application sections do not compare the clustering approach against any alternative or heuristic baseline.

weakness: The partitioning step may systematically exclude certain cross-applicants (e.g., different census tracts or varying income/credit score across applications), with no quantification of the resulting selection bias.
justification: Section 4.1 confirms partitioning is done on constant categorical variables like census tract, and the paper provides no quantification of applicants missed due to this partitioning.

weakness: Missing empirical comparison against the most closely related prior work (Alet et al. 2019, Hummos et al. 2024), despite claiming to 'greatly improve sample efficiency' over Alet et al.
justification: The paper (Discussion, lines 157-160) explicitly claims to replace Alet et al.'s search with probabilistic inference and 'greatly improve sample efficiency' but no experiment in the paper text compares against either Alet et al. or Hummos et al.

weakness: Evaluation scope is narrow relative to the paper's framing; both rule-learning and motor-learning tasks share the same combinatorial template (3 of N operations/skills with fixed 3/4/5-step durations), so generality is not well demonstrated.
justification: The paper text confirms both tasks use nearly identical structure (fixed skill/operation counts and durations of 3,4,5 steps) and itself calls the tasks 'proof-of-principle' (line 194), supporting the critique of narrow structural diversity.

weakness: Fixed number of modules matched to ground truth in main-text experiments; mismatch analysis is relegated to the appendix rather than summarized in the main text.
justification: The paper (line 91, Figure A1) confirms module-count mismatch results exist only in the appendix, and the main text does not summarize whether performance degrades gracefully.

weakness: The 'correlation' metric used for module/gating accuracy in Figure 2a is not specified.
justification: The paper's Figure 2a caption text (line 99) states accuracy is 'correlation with ground truth operations and transitions' without naming which correlation coefficient is used.

weakness: The paper's use of 'one-shot' terminology could be confused with standard few-shot-learning usage since a single episode is actually a full multi-timestep trajectory.
justification: The reviewer itself concedes 'Not a flaw, but the paper should distinguish its usage to avoid confusion' -- this is a terminology nitpick rather than a substantive weakness, and the paper's usage (inferring a task from a single episode) is clearly defined in context (Section 2.3).

weakness: The motor-learning model includes several domain-specific modifications (removing input x_t, resetting module hidden state, module-specific weights, different particle filter proposal) without discussing which are essential to the core framework versus merely convenient.
justification: The paper (line 127) lists these changes and explains the underlying differences motivating them, but does not discuss which modifications are strictly necessary versus incidental design choices, supporting this critique.

weakness: Causal attribution (softmax removal → poor locality) is confounded with Q/K binarization; no ablation isolates whether binarization vs softmax removal causes the locality loss.
justification: The paper's SSA (Eq.4-5) both binarizes Q/K/V via SN{} and removes softmax; Section 4.1/Theorem framing attributes the locality gap solely to softmax removal without any ablation isolating binarization, and no such control experiment appears in the paper text.

weakness: Theorems 1 and 2 describe LRF-SSA as interpolating with VSA weights (which require softmax), but the actual implementation (Eq. 8/14) never computes or interpolates with softmax-based VSA weights, and λ/α_i are undefined/untuned in experiments.
justification: Eq.8 and Eq.14 show LRF-SSA computed purely from SN{} dot products plus a convolution term with no softmax or λ interpolation, while Theorem 1 defines α^{lrf-ssa}=(1-λ)α^{vsa}+λr_ij using α^{vsa} which requires softmax (Eq.6); λ and α_i never appear again in Sections 5.3 or 6.

weakness: Energy-efficiency claims are made in abstract/intro without any energy, synaptic-operation, latency, or GPU memory measurement.
justification: The abstract and intro repeatedly invoke 'energy-efficient' and low-power computing, but Tables 1-3 and the text report only accuracy, parameter counts, and storage complexity (O notation), never actual measured energy, µJ, or memory in MB/GB.

weakness: The 'neuronal dynamics' framing of LRF-Dyn overclaims novelty since Eq. 11 is the standard causal linear-attention cumulative-sum trick that the paper itself cites (Katharopoulos et al., 2020) as prior work.
justification: Line 142 explicitly states LRF-Dyn is 'Inspired by other softmax-free attention (Yang et al., 2023; Zhang et al., 2024b; Shen et al., 2021)' and Eq.11's cumulative KV form matches known linear-attention causal reformulations, yet line 148 calls it 'a novel paradigm for self-attention computation.'

weakness: Table 2 has formatting inconsistencies: the SDT-V3 + LRF-SSA large-variant row shows '10.0 + 1.4M' parameters instead of the expected ~19M, inconsistent with the +LRF-Dyn row.
justification: Table 2 as reproduced in the paper text does show '10.0 + 1.4' for the SDT-V3+LRF-SSA large row versus '19.25 + 1.4' for the LRF-Dyn row, a genuine inconsistency given the base SDT-V3 large model uses 18.99M in Table 1.

weakness: The ablation (Table 3) compares LRF-Dyn against a weak 'Causal SSA' baseline that doesn't isolate what the A/Γ dendritic parameterization in Eq. 12 adds over a plain cumulative-sum linear attention (Eq. 11).
justification: Table 3 only reports LRF-SSA, LRF-Dyn, and 'Causal SSA' accuracies; there is no experiment directly comparing Eq.11 (plain cumulative sum) against Eq.12 (with learnable A, Γ) under identical settings, so the specific benefit of the neuronal-dynamics parameterization is not isolated in the paper.

weakness: Cross-reference error: the text refers to 'Table 4' when the table is actually labeled 'Table 1', and the phrase 'substantially outperforming models of comparable size' overstates a 0.92% gain.
justification: Line 188 in the paper text says 'As shown in Table 4' referencing what is captioned 'Table 1: Comparison with Similar Methods on ImageNet-1K', confirming the cross-reference error and the accompanying accuracy comparison (76.22% vs 75.30%, a 0.92-point gap) is a modest gain characterized as 'substantially outperforming.'

weakness: Fourier transform in Eq. 15 is introduced without clear motivation or explicit connection to the preceding recurrence derivation.
justification: Eq.15 introduces F, F^{-1}, and kernel K(t) with only a citation to Chen et al. 2024 and no textual explanation of why the FFT-based convolution formulation is needed or how it follows from Eq.12's recurrence.

weakness: Unclear treatment of test-set class priors in BEM (Eq. 9): ambiguous whether default initialization uses oracle test-set cardinalities or purely online-estimated priors, and no ablation/analysis of estimation quality is provided.
justification: Paper text at line 138 states priors are 'set to the cardinality of all classes ... in default' while also 'continually updated based on the current predicted pseudo-labels' — this is genuinely ambiguous, and no ablation comparing oracle vs. estimated priors or convergence analysis appears in the paper.

weakness: Hyperparameter inconsistency for K: implementation details (line 208) use K=0.3 as default, but the ablation (line 334) states K=0.2 yields the best performance, with no explanation for the discrepancy.
justification: Verified directly: line 208 sets K=0.3 as the default for main experiments, while line 334 explicitly says 'setting K = 0.2 yields the best performance,' and the paper gives no justification for using the suboptimal value in main results.

weakness: Missing variance statistics: tables report 5 runs but only point estimates, no standard deviations.
justification: Table captions (lines 154, 212, 246) state '5 runs' are conducted and averaged, but no standard deviation or error bars appear in the reported tables.

weakness: No failure-case analysis discussing settings where improvement is marginal or where the method underperforms baselines.
justification: The paper's results sections report averaged wins across benchmarks but do not include a dedicated discussion of cases with marginal or negative gains relative to baselines.

weakness: Theoretical propositions (Propositions 1-2) are relatively shallow, essentially direct consequences of definitions of entropy and the BEM penalty rather than deep theoretical results.
justification: Reviewing the propositions (lines 132-140) and their described logic, they follow fairly directly from the entropy gradient definition and penalty construction, supporting this critique as a reasonable qualitative assessment rather than a factual error.

weakness: Missing 'TTA + rebalancing' baseline (e.g., TPT + logit adjustment) to empirically support the claim that combining standard TTA with logit adjustment/balanced softmax exacerbates bias.
justification: Line 134 makes this claim in prose ('we may further exacerbate the model's bias toward the head classes') without pointing to a supporting experiment comparing TPT+logit-adjustment against L-TTA, so the claim is asserted but not empirically validated in the paper.

weakness: Corruption benchmark in the main paper only uses Gaussian noise (imb=10), with other 16 corruption types relegated to the appendix.
justification: Confirmed at line 206/246: the main Corruption Benchmark uses only Gaussian noise variations, while 'other 16 corruption types' are explicitly deferred to Appendix J.

weakness: The central robustness claim is underspecified because the paper repeatedly uses the term "meaningfully" without a pre-specified, falsifiable threshold, creating tension with the finding that additive/systematic perturbations qualitatively change the tokens-to-parameter trend.
justification: The paper text confirms both usages: it claims results "withstand sizable perturbations" (line 23) while also stating additive/systematic perturbations "can qualitatively change the compute-optimal scaling strategy by altering the trend" (line 23), and nowhere defines a numeric threshold for 'meaningfully.'

weakness: The additive constant perturbation, motivated as modeling embedding-parameter inclusion/exclusion, is unrealistic because embedding parameters scale with vocab size x d_model rather than being a constant offset across models from 44M to 16B parameters.
justification: The paper itself flags this as 'a simplification' (line 145) but does not discuss how the simplified constant-offset form affects interpretation, matching the reviewer's critique.

weakness: The paper does not explore what the best-fit coefficient of 5 (replacing 4) in the attention parameter formula corresponds to architecturally, leaving the source of the discrepancy unexplained.
justification: The paper reports the coefficient-5 best-fit formula reduces mismatches (lines 41, 64) but gives no architectural explanation (e.g., bias terms, separate Q/K projections) for why 5 rather than 4 fits better.

weakness: The sensitivity/perturbation analysis in Section 3 uses the standard formula parameters as baseline without justifying this choice, even though those are the parameters that mismatch Chinchilla's originally reported values.
justification: Line 102 confirms the standard formula parameters were used as the perturbation baseline ('we intentionally perturbed the standard formula model parameters'), and the paper does not justify this choice over using the reported-parameter baseline.

weakness: Policy evaluation results (Table 1) lack reported variance, confidence intervals, or trial counts in the main text, making it hard to assess stability of claimed performance gaps.
justification: Table 1 in the paper reports only single success-rate numbers with no error bars or trial counts described in the main text.

weakness: The abstract's claim that FASTerVQ 'encodes action chunks as single-channel images' is not substantiated in the method section, which only describes patchification and a hybrid transformer encoder without any image-specific processing.
justification: Section 3.1 describes an action patchifier and transformer encoder (line 54, 62) with no mention of single-channel image encoding or an image encoder, confirming the framing disconnect.

weakness: The lightweight action expert is underspecified: parameter count relative to backbone, architectural relationship, and joint vs staged training are not stated.
justification: Line 72 only says the expert shares 'the backbone architecture but with fewer parameters' inspired by π0, without giving parameter counts or training procedure details.

weakness: An unexplained performance regression occurs when BAR is added on the Simpler-Bridge 'Spoon' task (97.5% w/o BAR vs 91.7% with BAR), and this is not discussed in the paper.
justification: Table 1 line 150 shows FASTER w/o BAR at 97.5 on Spoon; the paper's text (line 308) only broadly attributes gains to the tokenizer without discussing this specific regression.

weakness: The spacing augmentation inference-time offset of 2 is not justified and no ablation is provided for this hyperparameter.
justification: Line 72 states 'At inference, we revert to a fixed spacing (e.g., p_i = p_{i-1} + 2)' without justification, and no ablation of this value appears in the main text (only Appendix A.3 is referenced generically for other ablations).

weakness: Non-Euclidean space framing is conceptually confused/overclaims; Rd with L2 norm is Euclidean and Mahalanobis distance is equivalent to Euclidean after linear whitening; KKT claim stated without proof.
justification: The paper explicitly claims KKT boundary conditions and max-margin classification are 'valid only in Euclidean vector spaces' (Lemma 2.1) without proof, and calls the input space non-Euclidean despite its own equation (1)/(2) showing it is a linear (whitening) transform of the same space, matching the review's critique exactly.

weakness: Inconsistency between Lemma 2.2 (predicting N/two linear classifiers) and the SM Algorithm which produces a single classifier with only the intercept adjusted.
justification: Lemma 2.2 states binary classification yields two classifiers, but SM Algorithm step (d)-(e) computes one theta_input classifier and only adjusts theta_0; the paper never reconciles this, as the review states.

weakness: No measure of variance or statistical significance across the 5 datasets; single 80/20 split, tiny reported improvements.
justification: Section 5 and Tables 1-4 report single-run point estimates with no confidence intervals or repeated splits, e.g. Pulsar accuracy 0.981 vs 0.979.

weakness: No hyperparameter tuning for kernel baselines (SVM-RBF, Poly, Sigmoid), disadvantaging them.
justification: The paper gives no description of any grid search or parameter selection for the baseline kernels in Section 5.

weakness: No empirical comparison against the most relevant prior covariance-aware SVM methods (MCVSVM, MD-TSVM, MD-BLSSVM) despite criticizing them in the Introduction.
justification: Section 1 criticizes these methods for 'gaps' and 'dimensional inconsistencies' but Section 5 only compares against linear/RBF/Sigmoid/Poly SVM and PCA/ZCA whitening, never against these cited methods.

weakness: No ablation studies isolating which component (whitening, margin-ratio adjustment, SM iteration) drives the results.
justification: The results section reports only the full CSVM-Cholesky pipeline versus baselines; no ablation of components is presented anywhere in the paper.

weakness: The criticism of prior work ('gaps in application of appropriate vector spaces and dimensional inconsistencies') is asserted but never elaborated with specifics for any cited work.
justification: Section 1 makes this claim in one sentence and Section 4 repeats a similar unsupported claim without ever identifying a concrete gap in any specific prior paper.

weakness: SM Algorithm's behavior is unanalyzed: no analysis of error propagation from mislabeled test data, no discussion of convergence to wrong labels, no comparison to a non-iterative baseline.
justification: Section 3 and Section 6 acknowledge the algorithm is 'heuristic' and that 'perfect classification is yet to be achieved' but provide no theoretical or empirical analysis of these specific concerns, and no non-iterative ablation is run.

weakness: Claim that 'the literature is divided on the reasons for [whitening improving SVM performance]' is unsupported by citation.
justification: Section 4 makes this claim without providing any reference, matching the review's observation exactly.

weakness: No dataset characteristics reported (size, features, class balance, preprocessing).
justification: Section 5 only names the five datasets without giving sample sizes, feature counts, class balance, or preprocessing steps.

weakness: No handling of singular covariance matrices discussed, a practical concern when per-class samples are fewer than features.
justification: Section 6 limitations discuss computational complexity and the SM algorithm's heuristic nature but never mention singular covariance matrices or small-sample-size issues.

weakness: Geometric interpretation of the margin in equation (9) is unclear/unjustified as a margin in the input space.
justification: Equation (9) is derived via a 'hypothetical' application of Cartesian geometry rules to the reverse-transformed classifier, and the paper does not justify why this quantity constitutes a meaningful margin in the original input space beyond that derivation.

weakness: Abstract claims 'accurate recovery of latent coefficients' but the quantitative evaluation only reports MMD_α (distributional similarity), not per-sample accuracy metrics (RMSE, correlation) even though ground-truth α is available in Darcy (drawn from a known GP).
justification: The paper only reports MMD_α, MMD_x, and residuals in its tables/figures (e.g. Table 1, 2, Fig. 3, 5); no per-sample RMSE/correlation/SSIM-to-ground-truth metric is reported anywhere in the text for Darcy despite ground truth α being available.

weakness: Baseline comparisons are too narrow: main comparisons are against the paper's own ablations, PBFM is augmented with the authors' φ, FM+ECI only appears in elasticity, and for Stokes PBFM fails to converge with base FM omitted, leaving mostly ablations.
justification: This is directly confirmed by the text: Sec 4 states PBFM is 'augmented with our pre-trained φ', FM+ECI appears only in Table 1 (elasticity), and Sec 4.5 explicitly states 'the base FM model exhibits extremely large residuals ... and is omitted for clarity, while PBFM fails to converge'.

weakness: Natural-image experiment (Sec 4.6) lacks quantitative rigor, providing only qualitative visual comparison with no FID/CLIP/PickScore numbers despite claiming cross-domain utility.
justification: Sec 4.6 mentions PickScore is used as the optimization objective but no PickScore/FID numbers are reported in the results; only qualitative descriptions ('markedly more vibrant palettes') and Fig. 6 are given.
