justification: The paper's own Figure 1 table lists 'Proportion of Parallel Data' as 44% for all four listed datasets (ShareGPT Vicuna, MRC, RAG, Math-220K) with no explanation given for this uniformity.

weakness: Some figure captions are duplicated (Figure 1 caption appears twice in the extracted text).
justification: The reviewer's own phrasing ('in the extracted text') indicates this is an artifact of text extraction from the PDF, not a genuine flaw in the paper as authored.

weakness: Equation numbering is inconsistent: Eq. 1 is numbered but subsequent equations are not.
justification: The paper text shows Eqs. 1, 2, 3, and 4 are all explicitly numbered (lines with '(1)', '(2)', '(3)', '(4)'), contradicting the claim.

weakness: The paper requires validation on larger-scale multimodal benchmarks (e.g., VGGSound, AudioSet) because the three datasets used (CREMA-D, KS, MVSA) are small-scale.
justification: CREMA-D, Kinetic-Sound, and MVSA are the standard benchmarks used by the exact SOTA baselines the paper compares against (MLA, MMPareto, LFM), so demanding evaluation on VGGSound/AudioSet goes beyond the established evaluation protocol of this specific line of work.

weakness: Only audio-visual and text-image modality pairs are tested; applicability to other modality combinations (e.g., video-text, 3D+RGB) is unclear.
justification: The paper only reports experiments on CREMA-D, Kinetic-Sound (audio-video) and MVSA (image-text); no other modality combinations are evaluated, so this generalization gap is real.

weakness: Missing comparison with several relevant modality-imbalance methods (PMR, AGM, CML, MBSD) that are discussed in the related work section but not empirically compared, weakening the SOTA claim.
justification: Table 1 baselines list Sum, Concat, FiLM, BiGated, OGM-GE, QMF, MLA, MMPareto, LFM only; PMR, AGM, CML, and MBSD, which are explicitly discussed in Section 2, are absent from the comparison table.

weakness: The paper provides no analysis of training time, FLOPs, or parameter count compared to baselines, despite the added computational overhead of the two-stage pretraining, alternating updates, and secondary updates.
justification: No section of the paper reports efficiency metrics such as training time, FLOPs, or parameter counts for CCAT versus baselines.

weakness: Sensitivity to the regularization coefficient lambda (fixed at 0.001) is not analyzed, only LoRA rank and beta are grid-searched.
justification: The implementation details section only reports grid search over LoRA rank r and threshold beta (Table 3, Figure 4); lambda is stated as fixed at 0.001 with no sensitivity study provided.

weakness: The mutual information estimation in Eq. (5) is a heuristic log-sum-exp approximation whose relation to true mutual information and appropriateness is not justified beyond citing prior work.
justification: The paper presents Eq. (5) with only a citation to Zhou et al. (2025b) and no derivation or justification connecting the softmax-based formula to a rigorous mutual information estimator.

weakness: The secondary update mechanism, which reprocesses severely imbalanced samples with additional gradient updates, may introduce training instability or overfitting on those samples, but this is not discussed or analyzed in the paper.
justification: The paper describes the secondary update procedure (Section 3.3, Eq. 12) but includes no discussion of potential overfitting or catastrophic forgetting risks from these extra targeted updates.

weakness: Core technical components are largely adaptations of existing ideas: the unified ODE framework is standard, the full flow map is directly from CTM, and the advantage-weighted objective is a restatement of AWR/CRR.
justification: The paper itself acknowledges CTMs 'explicitly parameterize Φ(x_t,t,s)...This corresponds exactly to our Trajectory Consistency Loss' and Theorem 2 is described as the standard KL-regularized policy optimization solution, supporting the novelty critique.

weakness: Theorem 1 is essentially a standard ODE solver convergence result and Theorem 2 is a direct consequence of KL-regularized policy optimization from AWR/CRR/IQL; neither provides deep new insight.
justification: Theorem 1's proof sketch explicitly relies on standard Lipschitz/solver-order convergence arguments, and Theorem 2 is derived from the well-known KL-regularized optimal policy form, matching the reviewer's characterization.

weakness: The claim of 'perfect scores on several notoriously hard AntMaze tasks' is misleading since only antmaze-umaze achieves 100.0 while antmaze-md is 94.2 and antmaze-lp is 53.5.
justification: Table 2 confirms antmaze-u=100±0 but antmaze-md=94.2 and antmaze-lp=53.5, so the 'several' perfect-score claim is not supported by the paper's own results table.

weakness: Narrow evaluation scope: results limited to D4RL Gym and AntMaze, with no evaluation on Adroit, Kitchen, or MetaWorld to test long-horizon claims.
justification: Section 5 and the visible experiments only report Gym and AntMaze D4RL results; no Adroit/Kitchen/MetaWorld evaluation appears in the paper text.

weakness: Missing comparison of training/inference efficiency (wall-clock, FLOPs) against diffusion-based and consistency-based policies (D-QL, C-AC), despite the paper's central efficiency claim.
justification: The only timing numbers given are in the ablation (Table 3, GTP vs w/o score approximation), with no wall-clock comparison against D-QL or C-AC reported anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: The paper does not discuss why C-AC significantly outperforms GTP on halfcheetah-medium and halfcheetah-medium-replay.
justification: Table 2 shows C-AC beats GTP on halfcheetah-m (69.1 vs 53.9) and halfcheetah-mr (58.7 vs 50.8), and the results/analysis text does not address these specific underperformances.

weakness: The parameterization φ(x_t,t,s) in Eq. (3) has a potential division by zero when s=t since t/(t-s) diverges, limiting the times at which it can be evaluated.
justification: The paper explicitly addresses this by defining the s→t limit analytically in Eq. (5) and naming it the 'Inst Map' φ^inst, showing the singularity is handled rather than left unresolved.

weakness: The paper uses 5 sampling steps for GTP but does not justify why this is the right number or show sensitivity to the number of steps.
justification: The main text states 'diffusion policies and our GTP use K=5 sampling steps' without justification or a sensitivity analysis presented in the visible sections.

weakness: The dependency mechanism relies entirely on integer arithmetic substitutions, so it is unclear whether insights transfer to more natural, qualitative/logical multi-step reasoning scenarios not reducible to integer arithmetic.
justification: The paper's Algorithm 1 and Section 3.1 confirm dependencies are constructed purely via extracting integers and defining f_i(x) = x + (m_{i+1} - a_i); the paper does not discuss whether findings generalize beyond this synthetic numeric substitution scheme.

weakness: Training experiments are limited in scope: only one base model (R1-Qwen-7B) is trained, only on math tasks, with max composed query count of 4, undermining the 'scalable' claim.
justification: Section 4.3 confirms training is done only on R1-Qwen-7B with math data (Skywork-OR1-RL) and composed counts of 1, 2, 4, and a mixture up to 4; no training on code/agent domains or other model sizes is reported.

weakness: The paper does not systematically compare R-HORIZON's dependency-based composition to simply concatenating independent problems (as in NEST) or longer independent sequences, so the benefit of dependencies versus longer context is not isolated.
justification: NEST is only discussed in Related Work (Section 2.2) as concatenating independent questions; no experimental ablation comparing dependency-based composition to plain concatenation is presented anywhere in the paper.

weakness: On WebShaper, several models (e.g., o4-mini, DeepSeek-R1) show higher accuracy on composed queries (n=2,3) than on single queries (n=1), a non-monotonic anomaly the paper does not explain.
justification: Figure 3 table shows o4-Mini WebShaper going 43.7(n=1)->87.6(n=2)->84.4(n=3) and DeepSeek-R1 33.3(n=1)->42.7(n=2)->41.3(n=3); the paper's only WebShaper comment is about models losing tool-calling ability, which does not explain this specific non-monotonic increase.

weakness: The expected-accuracy metric (product of atomic pass rates) assumes independence and conflates failure due to compound reasoning length versus failure to handle dependencies, without disentangling the two.
justification: Equation 4 defines Acc_expected as a simple product of independent pass rates p_i, and the paper never separately attributes the actual-vs-expected gap to length-driven versus dependency-driven failure, despite reporting both a general gap and a separate 'Dependency Reasoning Error' category in Figure 5 without reconciling them.

weakness: Table/Figure 3 contains an impossible accuracy value (127.6 for Qwen3-32B on MATH500 n=4), suggesting a data/transcription error.
justification: The results table row for Qwen3-32B under MATH500 explicitly lists '98.1 | 91.7 | 51.7 | 127.6 | 60.2', an accuracy exceeding 100%, confirming the reviewer's observation.

weakness: The code and agentic task construction process is relegated to the appendix with limited detail in the main text, making it harder to assess dataset quality/validity compared to the math construction.
justification: Section 3.1 explicitly states 'For code and agentic tasks, we provide the construction process in Appendix A,' while the main text gives detailed algorithmic description only for the math construction (Seed Problem Filtering, Algorithm 1).

weakness: Limited generality claim: TNT is claimed to be 'a general training paradigm applicable to any deep memory module,' yet all TNT experiments are conducted only on the Titans architecture, without validation on TTT or Atlas.
justification: The paper explicitly claims generality ('TNT is a general training paradigm applicable to any deep memory module') in the intro and Section 5, but Table 2/3 and all TNT results use only Titans; TTT appears only as an unmodified baseline, not as a TNT-adapted model.

weakness: Baseline selection inflates speedup claims: the headline '17x faster' compares TNT (C_L=64) against Titans with chunk size 8, an intentionally slow configuration, and this comparison should be contextualized against more practical Titans configurations like C=256.
justification: Table 1 shows Titans C=128 already trains in 3.71 hrs vs the 19.48 hrs for C=8, meaning the true speedup over a more practical baseline is far smaller than 17x, and the paper does not explicitly discuss this weaker comparison in the text.

weakness: Fine-tuning Stage 2 details are sparse: the paper states fine-tuning requires 'only an additional 5% of the original pre-training compute' with a 'brief' schedule but does not report exact steps, learning rate, or whether the full dataset is reused, making replication difficult.
justification: The main text (Section 4.2 and 5.3) only vaguely describes Stage 2 as 'a small number of steps' and '5% of compute' without giving concrete step counts, LR schedule, or dataset details in the visible text.

weakness: No comparison to linear memory modules: the paper does not include a baseline like Mamba or Gated DeltaNet in the efficiency comparison to position TNT relative to the broader efficient sequence modeling landscape.
justification: Table 2 already includes DeltaNet and GatedDeltaNet, both linear memory modules, as baselines directly compared against TNT and Titans, contradicting the reviewer's claim that no such comparison exists.

weakness: Q-K projection overhead not quantified: the projection matrix involves a d x d running sum, and the paper should report the additional FLOPs or memory relative to the base memory module, especially for large d.
justification: Section 4.1.2 describes the Q-K projection as a running d x d sum maintained in constant size but gives no explicit FLOPs or memory overhead numbers relative to the base module.

weakness: The warm-starting requirement (fixing 90% of weights via α=0.9) undermines the core claim that constrained optimization is a scalable and effective alternative to greedy heuristics, since without it SparseFW performs worse than baselines.
justification: The paper itself states 'setting α = 0.0 (full FW without any fixed weights) consistently yields worse results than the baselines' and best results occur fixing 90% of weights, directly supporting this critique of the paper's own framing.

weakness: Inconsistent perplexity improvements: SparseFW often underperforms the baseline it warm-starts from (e.g., SparseFW (Wanda) at 50% sparsity on DeepSeek-7B: 7.89 vs Wanda's 7.79; on LLaMA-3-8B: 10.21 vs RIA's 9.88), without adequate explanation of when it helps vs hurts.
justification: Table 1 confirms these exact numbers (7.89 vs 7.79 and 10.21 vs 9.88), and the paper only broadly notes gains are 'much more consistent' at higher sparsity without explaining the 50% inconsistencies in detail.

weakness: Computational cost is not properly contextualized: the paper acknowledges SparseFW is 'clearly more compute-intensive than Wanda and RIA' but provides no runtime or FLOPs comparisons.
justification: The paper text explicitly states this compute-intensiveness (line 240) but nowhere reports wall-clock time or FLOPs comparisons against baselines.

weakness: The theoretical bound in Lemma 1 is stated informally and its key term is very large for LLM-scale dimensions, making the bound practically vacuous.
justification: The paper explicitly labels Lemma 1 as 'Informal' and defers the full statement to the appendix, and does not address the practical magnitude of the bound for LLM-scale d_in/d_out.

weakness: The paper does not compare to SparseGPT, one of the most popular LLM pruning methods, though the reviewer notes the given justification is reasonable.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'we hence do not compare directly to methods that involve a reconstruction step, such as SparseGPT', confirming the omission, which the review correctly notes and reasonably contextualizes.

weakness: The ablation of α (fraction of fixed weights) is relegated to the appendix despite its critical importance, and should be a main-text figure.
justification: The paper states 'We ablate the impact of this ratio in Table 2 in the appendix,' confirming this important ablation is not in the main text.

weakness: The paper uses 'pruning error' and 'reconstruction error' somewhat interchangeably without precise definition.
justification: The paper uses both terms (e.g., 'per-layer pruning error' and 'reconstruction error' in Figure 2's caption/title) without an explicit definitional distinction between them.

weakness: Overclaimed 'inductive bias' interpretation - IICLL convergence could reflect statistical patterns implicitly encoded in training rather than an independent bias, so the term 'inductive bias' is stronger than evidence supports.
justification: The paper acknowledges this is an open question itself ('the precise origins of the bias we observe in LLMs toward efficiency are unclear... how might this bias emerge from properties of the training data') and does not rule out training-data explanations, so the critique that the strong 'inductive bias' language outpaces the evidence is well grounded.

weakness: Generality limited by reliance on a single model - only Gemini 2.0 reproduces the full human range of IB tradeoffs while other strong models converge to low-complexity solutions, and the title/abstract understate this limitation.
justification: This is explicitly true per the paper text: 'only a model with strongest in-context capabilities (Gemini 2.0) is able to recapitulate the wide range of near-optimal IB-tradeoffs... while other state-of-the-art models converge to low-complexity solutions,' yet the abstract frames the finding broadly as an LLM-general capacity.

weakness: Shepard circles analysis is preliminary and not tied to IB - lacks quantitative IB evaluation, making the 'may generalize beyond color' claim unsupported.
justification: The paper itself admits this limitation: 'An important direction for future work is to test whether this emergent structure also supports greater IB-efficiency as seen in humans,' confirming no IB evaluation was done for Shepard circles.

weakness: Inconsistent presentation of human IL data - Figure 3 shows only final-generation human IL points while LLM trajectories show intermediate generations, weakening the visual comparison.
justification: The paper confirms this directly: 'Figure 3 shows our reproduction of this finding (plotting only final generations)' for human IL data, while LLM trajectories are shown as full trajectories across generations.

weakness: Lack of formal statistical testing - improvement over IICLL generations (Figure 4) shown with confidence intervals but no formal hypothesis tests against null models like random drift or rotation baselines.
justification: The paper explicitly reports a rotation analysis (Regier et al., 2007) testing significance of emergent systems against rotated baselines, finding 'a significant decrease in efficiency and alignment for Gemini,' which the reviewer overlooks.

weakness: The architectures used for SGDL and MGDL are not matched in depth, capacity, or parameter count (e.g., SGDL 8 hidden layers vs MGDL 4 grades x 2 hidden layers each; SGT deep stack vs MGT single-block sequential), confounding the multi-grade effect with depth effect.
justification: Paper Section 5 explicitly states SGDL uses architecture (2,1,128,8) while MGDL uses (2,1,128,2,4), and Section 8 confirms SGT trains a deep stack of n_h blocks at once while MGT trains single-block transformers sequentially, so the comparison indeed does not control for total depth/capacity.

weakness: Theorems 1 and 2 assume the activation is twice continuously differentiable, but ReLU (used throughout experiments) is not, and this mismatch is unaddressed.
justification: The paper states 'σ is twice continuously differentiable' as a hypothesis in Theorem 1/2, yet all experiments (Sections 5-8) use ReLU activations, and no discussion reconciles this gap.

weakness: The convexity result (Theorem 3) is essentially a direct per-grade application of Pilanci & Ergen (2020), and the claimed 'extension from shallow to deep architectures' is just the multi-grade decomposition already defined in Section 3.
justification: The paper itself says the convex program 'following Pilanci & Ergen (2020)' is applied per grade, and the multi-grade decomposition was already introduced in Section 3, supporting the reviewer's characterization.

weakness: The eigenvalue analysis (Theorem 4/Section 7) is heuristic, linearizing the gradient without rigorously proving MGDL's eigenvalues always stay within (-1,1) while SGDL's do not, and empirical eigenvalue plots use very small networks (e.g., 48 hidden units).
justification: Section 7 states the linearization 'neglects r^{k-1}' and the image regression eigenvalue experiment explicitly uses architecture (2,1,48,4)/(2,1,48,1,4), i.e., small shallow networks, confirming the review's claim.

weakness: For CIFAR-100 the paper only reports training loss (Figure 3) with no test accuracy reported, making the practical benefit for classification unsubstantiated.
justification: Section 5's CIFAR-100 paragraph and Figure 3 caption only discuss training loss values, with no mention of test/validation accuracy anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: For the CIFAR-10 eigenvalue analysis, only training loss is shown, and the setting (fully connected network, 10,000 samples, full-batch GD, MSE loss) is far from standard classification practice, so no test accuracy is given.
justification: Section 7's CIFAR-10 paragraph explicitly describes '10,000 sampled images, fully connected ReLU networks... trained with squared loss and full-batch gradient descent' and reports only training loss values, matching the review's description.

weakness: The paper does not discuss or compare against boosting, gradient boosting, or residual learning (ResNets), which are conceptually close to MGDL's residual-training approach, leaving novelty unclear.
justification: No mention of boosting, gradient boosting, or ResNet-style residual learning appears anywhere in the visible paper text (including related work/citations), so this comparison is indeed absent.

weakness: The claim that MGDL is a 'scalable framework' is not backed by experiments on modern large-scale architectures or datasets (e.g., ImageNet, large transformers); experiments use small networks (e.g., 128 hidden units, 4 grades) and limited datasets.
justification: The abstract asserts MGDL is a 'scalable framework,' yet all reported experiments use small networks such as (2,1,128,2,4) or (3072,10,128,2,4) on CIFAR-10/100 and small image sets, with no large-scale dataset or model evaluation shown.

weakness: The paper often writes equations without fully specifying dimensions, and some notation (e.g., the recursive definition in Eq. (3)) is hard to follow.
justification: Eq. (3)'s recursive definition of g_{l+1} indeed involves nested composition notation with dimensions not spelled out inline, supporting the specific complaint about that equation.

weakness: The 'single-grade' vs 'multi-grade' terminology is non-standard and could cause confusion with existing literature on curriculum learning or stagewise training.
justification: This terminology is inherited from the established MGDL literature (Xu 2025, Fang & Xu 2024) that the paper builds on and cites, so objecting to naming consistency with prior work is not a substantive flaw of this paper.

weakness: The claim that the loss bump in Figure 6 resembles induction head formation is speculative, based only on loss curve shape without attention pattern analysis or mechanistic verification.
justification: The paper itself only hedges with 'we hypothesize' and 'this bump resembles' (line 188) without providing attention-pattern or causal-tracing evidence, so the critique that this interpretation lacks mechanistic verification is accurate.

weakness: The paper's core claims about optimization instability and scaling behavior are demonstrated only on synthetic benchmarks (MQAR and copying), limiting immediate practical impact.
justification: Confirmed by the paper's own conclusion (line 235): 'we acknowledge that our analysis is conducted on synthetic benchmarks... Validating these dynamics on downstream language modeling tasks is a critical next step.'

weakness: All experiments use only the Adam optimizer; other optimizers (SGD with momentum, different AdamW schedules) that could mitigate the narrow learning rate window for SSMs are not explored.
justification: Confirmed by line 193 which states the optimization algorithm used throughout is Adam, and the paper does not report experiments with alternative optimizers.

weakness: The claim of state-of-the-art is not fully supported for all settings; e.g., in Table 2, Base LRS3 (low-resource) USR 2.0 gets 36.2% VSR vs USR's 36.0%, a worse result, and ASR/AVSR gains there are marginal.
justification: Table 2 (Base, LRS3 row) indeed shows USR 2.0 at V=36.2 vs USR at V=36.0, a genuine regression, while A/AV gains in that row are 3.0 vs 3.2 and 2.9 vs 3.0 -- small margins, supporting the critique that SOTA claims are strongest only for larger models/more pretraining data.

weakness: The mixed sampling AR probability is a significant hyperparameter with no principled guidance on how to tune it for new datasets/tasks, since ID and OOD performance trade off oppositely with it (Figure 4).
justification: The paper only states the probability 'may be tuned to match application needs, with our default of 0.5 offering a strong overall balance' (Section 7), without a principled method or heuristic for setting it per dataset, matching the reviewer's concern.

weakness: The claim that 'global coherence is unnecessary' in the pseudo-labelling setting is not rigorously justified with a formal analysis or controlled experiment beyond the empirical results.
justification: Section 4.1's justification is an intuitive argument about matched conditioning; the paper points to Appendix C.4 'for discussion' rather than a controlled ablation isolating the coherence effect, so the reviewer's request for stronger justification is grounded.

weakness: The comparison to USR in Table 2 for the Base model on LRS3 shows USR 2.0 is worse for VSR (36.2 vs 36.0), which is not explicitly acknowledged or discussed in the text.
justification: The main text's discussion of Table 2 (Section 6) only states USR 2.0 'matches or outperforms the state of the art' without flagging this specific regression, so the omission is real, though this duplicates the first major weakness.

weakness: The paper does not report confidence intervals or statistical significance for any results, despite some comparisons differing by only 0.1-0.2% WER.
justification: No section of the paper reports variance, multiple seeds, or significance tests for the WER numbers in Tables 1-4, so this is a genuine gap given the small margins reported (e.g., Table 2 Base+ AV: 1.4 vs 1.3).

weakness: The OOD evaluation on AVSpeech uses only 1,000 manually filtered samples transcribed by Whisper, and the filtering/transcription process could introduce bias with a small sample size.
justification: Section 5.3 confirms AVSpeech evaluation uses '1,000 manually filtered AVSpeech samples... transcribed using Whisper,' a relatively small, manually curated set whose filtering criteria are not detailed, supporting the reliability concern.

weakness: The comparison between GPA and the TRAIL baseline is unfair/confounded since GPA uses seven specialized judges with custom architecture descriptions and few-shot examples, while no ablation isolates the structural decomposition (multi-judge) from better prompting/context.
justification: The paper reports baseline variants with and without control-flow/architecture description (Table 2, 5), but never ablates the effect of using multiple specialized judges versus a single judge given the same context, so the core criticism about missing ablation stands.

weakness: Plan Quality and Plan Adherence judges perform poorly on the primary dataset (low F1/precision, small sample sizes), undermining their inclusion as core validated components.
justification: Tables 3 and 6 confirm PQ has F1=0.49 (test) and PA has precision ~0.52, and the paper itself acknowledges 'PQ's poor metrics again confirm its unreliability' and notes 'small sample size...makes it difficult to evaluate these LLM Judges reliably.'

weakness: The experiments rely on Claude-4-Sonnet and Claude-Sonnet-4.5, unreleased/proprietary models at review time, hurting reproducibility, and no results are shown with a widely available model.
justification: The paper states 'we use Claude-4-Sonnet' and 'Claude-Sonnet-4.5' throughout Section 4 with no experiments on any other publicly available model, supporting the reproducibility concern.

weakness: The internal ANON-Data-Agent dataset is very small (17 traces), limiting statistical power for per-metric conclusions.
justification: The paper explicitly states the internal dataset consists of '17 agent traces,' confirming the small sample size.

weakness: The GEPA meta-judge used to grade GPA judges' outputs is itself an LLM judge with no independent verification against human annotations, raising a circularity concern.
justification: Section 4.1.5 describes the meta-judge as 'a strongly aligned LLM judge verifier' used to grade GPA judges, but the paper provides no human-validation check specifically on the meta-judge's own accuracy.

weakness: The Goal Fulfillment (GF) judge is named as a core framework component but receives little to no quantitative experimental treatment compared to the other five judges.
justification: GF appears in Figure 1 and Section 3 as a key judge, but Tables 3, 4, 6, and 8 (all main quantitative results) only report LC, EE, PA, PQ, TS, and TC, with no GF results anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: The term 'GPA' is an overloaded acronym (commonly 'grade point average'), which may cause confusion.
justification: This is a trivial naming quibble unrelated to the paper's technical merit and does not constitute a substantive weakness of the work.

weakness: Heuristic switching criterion (entropy comparison in Eq. 2-3) lacks theoretical justification and is not compared to alternative confidence measures (e.g., top-token probability, softmax calibration, predictive variance); asymmetric dwell windows lack principled derivation.
justification: The paper only motivates the entropy criterion and asymmetric windows via intuition (Sec 3.3, 'Our key insight is...') without theoretical analysis or comparison to alternative confidence signals.

weakness: Incomplete specification of the early-answer mechanism: unclear how the injection queue interacts with the model's own answer generation, and no analysis of correctness/robustness of forced early answering.
justification: Sec 3.4 describes the injection queue mechanically but never analyzes whether forced termination produces nonsensical outputs or how often the convergence trigger yields correct answers.

weakness: Method has several hyperparameters (dwell window, alpha0, beta0, C_max) with significant sensitivity, but no guidance for setting them on new tasks/models without a validation set; linear scheduling of alpha_t/beta_t is not justified.
justification: Table 2 shows beta0 sensitivity from 39% to 63% average accuracy, and the paper explicitly says values are chosen via ablation/exposed to users for adjustment (Sec 4.5), with no principled scheduling justification given.

weakness: Token efficiency metric interpretation is unclear: large reported gains (e.g., +213% on GPQA Diamond) may be inflated by choice of denominator (CoT's plain efficiency at peak) or by very small budgets where CoT accuracy is near zero; a direct accuracy-at-fixed-token-budget comparison would be clearer.
justification: The metric definition in Sec 4.1 normalizes by CoT's peak efficiency and integrates over budgets, but the paper never analyzes sensitivity to this choice or provides fixed-budget accuracy comparisons.

weakness: The paper derives a closed-form MSE-optimal α (Theorem 2) but does not explain how α is chosen/estimated in the experiments, making the 'MSE-optimal' claim disconnected from the actual implementation and the results not faithfully reproducible.
justification: The paper's Section 5.1 (Experiment Settings) and the excerpted text describe training data, model, and evaluation setup but never state how α is set or estimated in practice; Theorem 2's formula requires biases and covariances (b_t, b_e, Σ_t, Σ_e, Σ_te) that are not computed or discussed anywhere in the provided text, so this is a genuine, verifiable gap.

weakness: Restriction to one-layer, linear-attention architectures limits applicability to practical multi-layer, multi-head, softmax-based models used in practice.
justification: The paper itself acknowledges this in Remark 6 and Section 5, explicitly limiting the comparison to one-layer single-head linear attention and noting future work needed for general Mamba-based models.

weakness: Highly synthetic data model with orthogonal relevant/irrelevant/outlier patterns limits direct applicability of the quantitative bounds to real-world text, with real-data experiments relegated to the appendix.
justification: Section 3.2 defines the data model using strictly orthogonal patterns with controlled magnitudes, and the main text footnote confirms additional real-world experiments are only in Appendix B.2, supporting the critique.

weakness: The theorems rely on numerous conditions with implicit constants and Θ/≳/≲ notation that are intertwined and hard to interpret as actionable design rules.
justification: Theorems 1-4 indeed use asymptotic notation with unspecified constants and coupled conditions (e.g., condition (iii) in Theorem 1 links l_tr and M_1^{kappa_a}), confirming the critique.

weakness: The comparison Transformer model (linear attention with gating fixed to 1) is arguably too weak since it lacks softmax normalization that could help real Transformers handle outliers.
justification: The paper acknowledges this exact limitation in Remark 6, stating the comparison isolates linear attention vs. gating and that softmax/multi-head discussion is deferred to the appendix.

weakness: Figure 2 axes are not uniformly labeled and the caption is repeated three times without clearly distinguishing the subplots.
justification: The paper text shows the Figure 2 caption text is indeed duplicated verbatim across the figure description, supporting this minor presentation critique.

weakness: Missing error bars and statistical significance across multiple runs/seeds for main results.
justification: The paper reports single-number results in Tables 1-3 with no mention of seeds, standard deviations, or multiple runs anywhere in the text.

weakness: Limited architectural scope: all experiments use CLIP ViT-B/16, with no experiments on larger VLMs (ViT-L, ViT-g, SigLIP), and the claim that scaling behavior extends naturally is speculative.
justification: The paper itself states 'While our empirical results focus on ViT-B/16, the same scaling behavior extends naturally to larger CLIP variants' without any supporting experiment, confirming this is an unverified claim.

weakness: Theoretical contribution (Lemma 1, Theorem 2) is modest, bounding parameter-space interference as a straightforward consequence of SVD construction rather than providing function-level guarantees or deep insight into forgetting dynamics.
justification: The paper explicitly concedes this: 'the above results are stated in parameter space and should be viewed as a local stability condition rather than a full function-level guarantee... Deriving tighter, function-level forgetting bounds remains an interesting direction for future work.'

weakness: The 'zero auxiliary model load' claim is slightly imprecise since null-space bases (U_n, V_n) are computed and stored per task as part of model weights, and this should be clarified as memory-free for external storage only.
justification: This is a fair nuanced reading; the paper's claims of 'zero storage overhead, zero auxiliary model load' are about external memory (replay buffers/gradient memories per line 50), and the reviewer correctly notes the bases are still part of the persisted model, a legitimate clarification request.

weakness: The forgetting metric used in Figure 3a ('average drop from post-task to final performance') is not fully defined with an exact formula in the paper.
justification: The paper only gives the informal description at line 254 ('Forgetting (defined as the average drop from post-task to final performance)') with no explicit mathematical formula provided in the main text.

weakness: Insufficient comparison to state-of-the-art latent generative models (LDM, LSGM, VDM) in the main paper; only observation-space SI models are compared in the core experiments, and the comparison to other methods is relegated to an appendix (section R).
justification: The paper's main text (Table 1) only compares LSI against observation-space SI models trained at matched size; the comparison to other latent generative baselines is only referenced as being in an appendix, so the core paper's claim of 'competitive generative performance' vs. the broader latent-model literature is not substantiated in the main results.

weakness: The linear drift and additive noise assumption (Eq. 7) needed for tractable Gaussian transitions is a significant restriction relative to the full generality of SI, and the tradeoff between tractability and flexibility is under-discussed.
justification: The paper explicitly acknowledges this restriction and its implication multiple times: 'the assumptions made for eq. (7), while restrictive, do not limit the empirical performance' and again in the Conclusion ('our approach makes simplifying assumptions... While restrictive... these assumptions do not seem to limit the empirical performance'), directly addressing the tradeoff the reviewer claims is missing.

weakness: The relationship of the InterpFlow parameterization to well-known parameterizations (e.g., velocity/noise prediction) is not fully clarified, making it hard to situate LSI relative to existing diffusion/flow-matching methods.
justification: The paper states it 'consider[s] several alternative parameterizations for the second term, including denoising and noise prediction (see section C for details)' and Table 3 directly compares InterpFlow against OrigFlow, NoisePred, and Denoising, showing the reviewer overlooked this explicit comparison.

weakness: Limited discussion of hyperparameter sensitivity: optimal beta and encoder noise scale appear dataset-specific with little practical guidance for choosing them on new datasets.
justification: The paper only reports ablation curves for beta and c at one resolution/dataset (Figure 1) without providing selection heuristics or guidance for new settings, supporting this critique.

weakness: Qualitative results for CFG and inversion sampling (Figures 2 and 3) are illustrative but lack quantitative evaluation (e.g., FID vs. guidance strength, reconstruction fidelity).
justification: Section 6's discussion of Figures 2 and 3 provides only qualitative visual examples with no accompanying quantitative metrics for these sampling modes, confirming the gap.

weakness: The paper's claim of "exact density evaluation" is misleading, since the density in Eq. 2 is a Monte Carlo average over Nc samples from q_theta(w), making it a stochastic finite-sample estimator rather than a deterministic value, and this conflates the model definition with its practical implementation.
justification: The paper repeatedly claims 'efficient exact likelihood' and 'exact density evaluation by construction' (Table 1, Introduction, Conclusion), yet Eq. 2 explicitly defines q_theta(x) as a finite average over resampled w_i, and the paper nowhere discusses the variance of this estimator or gives guidance on choosing Nc.

weakness: The only high-dimensional experiments are in VAE latent spaces of dimension 10-20, not on raw high-dimensional data (e.g., pixels), so scaling to realistic high-dimensional densities is not demonstrated; the Wishart experiment reaches d=5050 but on an extremely low-dimensional (1D) manifold, a very structured problem.
justification: Section 4.4 confirms latent spaces are only 20- and 10-dimensional, and Section 4.3 confirms the Wishart manifold is 1D; no experiment demonstrates general high-dimensional density estimation without such structure.

weakness: The MNIST and JAFFE examples are purely qualitative (manifold interpolation) with no likelihood numbers, sample quality metrics, or comparisons to other density models on these datasets.
justification: Section 4.4 only shows qualitative grids of interpolated digits/faces (Figures 10-11) with no quantitative likelihood or metric reported, and no baseline comparison for these datasets.

weakness: The paper asserts universality for kernel choices (citing Micchelli et al., 2006) but provides no proof or discussion of required conditions, and the expressivity of the model for general high-dimensional distributions is not analyzed.
justification: Section 2.1 states 'the resulting marginal q(x) is universal for many families of distributions q(x|w), e.g. if q(x|w) is a kernel (Micchelli et al., 2006)' as a bare assertion with a citation but no derivation or conditions given in the visible text.

weakness: The paper does not discuss the variance of the density estimator or how to set Nc in practice for reliable log-likelihood evaluation, which is especially relevant for test-set evaluation and comparison to deterministic models.
justification: This is a restatement of the fatal flaw finding; no discussion of Nc selection or estimator variance appears anywhere in the main text provided.

weakness: The term "Marginal Flow" is somewhat misleading since no "flow" transformation of densities is involved.
justification: This is explicitly flagged by the reviewer themselves as 'a minor nomenclature issue' — a trivial naming critique that is not a substantive flaw in the paper's content or methodology.

weakness: SAE experiments are conducted only on Llama3.1-8B with a single SAE (Goodfire's, trained on layer 19), limiting generality of claims about SAE-based steering danger.
justification: Paper explicitly states in Sec 3.3: 'we limited our investigation of SAE feature steering to this specific model and layer,' confirming the scope limitation is real.

weakness: The universal attack construction (Sec 4.4) does not ablate the number of vectors averaged (e.g., 5, 10, 50) nor test whether vectors must jailbreak the same prompt.
justification: The paper fixes the number at 20 ('we select 20 vectors...a number chosen to balance attack potency and sampling efficiency') without any reported sweep over other counts or cross-prompt vector mixing.

weakness: No quantitative comparison to existing gradient-based or optimization-based jailbreak methods (e.g., GCG, PAIR) to contextualize the threat level.
justification: Figure 6 only compares random, individual unsafe, and averaged unsafe directions; no established external jailbreak baseline is reported anywhere in the paper.

weakness: Reliance on a single judge model (Qwen3-8B) for all 300,000 responses without a human or second-model spot-check to validate compliance rate measurements.
justification: Sec 3.4 states Qwen3-8B is the sole judge model used; the paper mentions quality assessment against human annotations only in an appendix reference, not as a validating spot-check in the main text, so the concern about single-judge bias is grounded.

weakness: The paper does not systematically explore how non-monotonic degradation of output coherence at high steering coefficients affects compliance rate validity, since incoherent outputs are always classified SAFE, potentially masking true vulnerability.
justification: Sec 3.4 confirms 'Incoherent, repetitive, or nonsensical responses are always classified as SAFE, even if they mention harmful content,' and the paper notes 'excessive coefficients degrade output coherence' without further systematic analysis of this interaction.

weakness: Figure 2 caption text repeats the description in the main text without adding new information, making it unnecessarily verbose.
justification: Comparing the Figure 2 caption text to the surrounding prose confirms substantial overlap/redundancy, a minor but accurate stylistic observation.

weakness: Unconditional generation performance gap: model underperforms HierVAE substantially on molWt, TPSA, MR; the early-termination explanation is plausible but not empirically validated with quantitative analysis.
justification: The paper's Limitations section (Sec 5) only offers a hypothesis about early termination without any quantitative evidence (e.g., molecule size distributions) to support it, so the review's call for empirical validation is well grounded.

weakness: Limited baseline comparisons for unconditional generation: only HierVAE is compared, MARS and MoLeR are excluded, and additional baselines like JTNN, G-SchNet, or diffusion models are not included.
justification: The paper indeed only reports quantitative comparison against HierVAE in Table 1 and relegates MoLeR to an appendix due to poor results; JTNN/G-SchNet are discussed only qualitatively in related work, not benchmarked, so the single-baseline concern is accurate.

weakness: Conditional generation evaluation lacks any comparison baselines (e.g., conditional VAEs, property-conditional diffusion, RL-based approaches), making it hard to assess whether calibration quality is a meaningful advance.
justification: Section 4.3 presents only MolMiner's own calibration plots (Figure 2) with no comparison to any other conditional generative model, confirming the gap the reviewer identifies.

weakness: Limited analysis of failure cases: systematic deviations for QED, molWt, and MR are only briefly hypothesized rather than deeply analyzed (e.g., correlation structure among properties, data distribution characteristics).
justification: Section 5 gives only a one-paragraph hypothesis about termination bias for molWt/TPSA/MR and does not address QED's calibration degradation at all, supporting the claim that failure-case analysis is shallow.

weakness: No explicit validity metric reported, even though the paper claims the model 'consistently produces valid molecules.'
justification: The paper explicitly justifies omitting validity because valence constraints are enforced during generation ('We omit validity, as our model enforces valence constraints during generation and consistently produces valid molecules'), a structural guarantee that makes reporting a validity percentage unnecessary busywork rather than a real gap.

weakness: Computational cost (7 days training on RTX 3090, 70GB RAM) may limit reproducibility and adoption, and the paper doesn't discuss smaller/more efficient variants.
justification: The paper's Computational Requirements section (Sec 7) confirms these figures and indeed contains no discussion of lighter-weight variants, so the observation is accurate.

weakness: The paper claims to be first to unify several capabilities but does not provide a systematic comparison table showing which prior models have which capabilities.
justification: The related work section makes these claims only in prose (Sec 2), with no table contrasting capabilities across JTNN, HierVAE, G-SchNet, and MoLeR, so the suggestion identifies a genuine presentational gap.

weakness: Missing comparison to existing multi-task codec works (Chamain et al. 2021, Feng et al. 2022, Guo et al. 2024) despite citing them, leaving unclear whether the Gray-Wyner design offers benefits beyond simpler multi-task codecs.
justification: The paper explicitly discusses these works in Section 2 ('Multitask learnable codecs exist in the literature (Chamain et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2024)...') but the experiments in Section 4 only compare against Joint and Independent baselines, never these cited multi-task codecs.

weakness: The common channel construction mechanism (Eq. 14, averaging matching elements / zeroing otherwise) with auxiliary loss (Eq. 15, γ=1) is heuristic/ad-hoc and not theoretically justified, potentially limiting robustness.
justification: The paper itself describes this as a workaround ('We overcome this obstacle in practice by setting γ = 1...') without deriving it from the theory in Theorem 1/2, matching the reviewer's characterization.

weakness: Theorem 1's bounds on lossy common information are not empirically verified against the learned representations, leaving a weak connection between theory and experiments.
justification: Section 4 reports rate-distortion curves and BD-rates but never computes interaction information of learned representations to check against Theorem 1's bounds, as the reviewer states.

weakness: The architecture description (Figure 2, mask block, how Y0 is used as context for private entropy models) is confusing and lacks a step-by-step explanation.
justification: While Section 3.3 gives some textual description of the conditioning, the 'mask' block in Figure 2 is never explicitly explained in the text, supporting the reviewer's clarity concern.

weakness: Pre-trained task models (DeepLabV3+, Faster R-CNN, etc.) are kept frozen during codec training, and the paper does not discuss whether fine-tuning them would change the tradeoff.
justification: The paper states 'We keep their weights fixed as we train the rest of the codec' (Section 4.3) and provides no discussion of fine-tuning these models, confirming the reviewer's point.

weakness: The claim of an average -81.58% BD-rate advantage 'against single-task codecs' is reported without a clear definition of 'single-task codecs' and without error bars or statistical significance.
justification: The summary (Section 5) states this number but never explicitly defines which baseline 'single-task codecs' refers to, nor does the paper report confidence intervals for BD-rate values anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: The receive rate definition (2R0+R1+R2) assumes both tasks are received separately, which is a specific operational scenario that the paper does not caveat as one option among others.
justification: The paper presents Rr = 2R0+R1+R2 as the receive rate definition (Section 2.1) without noting alternative definitions, matching the reviewer's minor observation.

weakness: The median BWR values (0.54-0.62) are only modestly above 0.50 and the paper lacks a concrete cost-benefit analysis (wall-clock time or FLOP savings) showing whether this translates to meaningful practical savings given the overhead of the two-stage procedure and Monte Carlo estimation.
justification: The paper reports these BWR ranges in Table 1 and nowhere provides wall-clock or FLOP overhead analysis of the KDE fitting and Monte Carlo estimation steps.

weakness: The paper only compares against uniform allocation, with no comparison to other adaptive test-time compute approaches, no ablation of the greedy allocation versus simpler heuristics, and no comparison to simply using a smaller uniform budget.
justification: The paper's own related work section acknowledges Damani et al. (2024) as the only closely related adaptive method and explicitly states they did not compare against it or any other adaptive baseline/heuristic.

weakness: The exploration budget d=0.75B is a critical hyperparameter but not thoroughly studied, and this conservative split limits potential gains from adaptivity.
justification: The paper explicitly studies this in Section 4.3 ('AdaBoN requires minimal hyperparameter tuning') and Appendix G.1/Table 3, tuning d over {0.60B, 0.70B, 0.75B, 0.80B} and showing the choice incurs minimal drop from optimal — this is exactly the kind of study the reviewer claims is missing.

weakness: With K=5, B=120, d=0.75B, only 30 samples per prompt remain for adaptive allocation across 5 prompts, so gains from redistribution may be inherently limited, and the empirical setting may favor the method.
justification: This is an accurate arithmetic observation about the paper's main experimental configuration (Section 4.3) and a reasonable interpretive concern not addressed by the authors.

weakness: The paper does not analyze what properties of a batch (e.g., variance, multi-modality of reward distributions) drive AdaBoN's success, limiting practical guidance for practitioners.
justification: While Appendix G.1 explains one specific case (Qwen-Armo underperforming due to left-skew), the paper provides no general characterization of which batch/distribution properties predict larger gains.

weakness: The EST definition bounds the sum to 2B, making the maximum observable EST around 240, yet reported values cluster around 148-153, providing limited resolution for differentiation.
justification: The paper states in Section 4.3 that 'We estimate the EST by capping the sum in Equation 5 to 2B,' and Table 2a reports EST medians in the 148-153 range, supporting the reviewer's resolution concern.

weakness: Abstract/intro claim that F2F improves calibration on medical QA tasks (reducing overconfidence) is unsubstantiated because no calibration metrics (ECE, reliability diagrams) appear anywhere in the main paper.
justification: The abstract states F2F 'helps improved calibration on medical QA tasks, reducing overconfidence' but Section 4 only reports pass@1 accuracy tables and CKA/SVCCA analysis; no calibration metric or figure is presented in the main text.

weakness: The theoretical analysis (Proposition/Corollary) relies on strong-convexity and linear-model assumptions that do not hold for LLMs, and is presented as if it explains the empirical results despite the mismatch.
justification: The paper itself admits 'While LLM training objective is non-convex, we use a convex linear surrogate to clarify the mechanism' (Sec 2), confirming the assumptions are a stylized approximation rather than a guarantee for the actual non-convex LLM setting.

weakness: The forget set is drawn from BookCorpus (fiction/narrative), which is not representative of the general pretraining data of modern LLMs, and only 100-1000 samples are used to 'remove irrelevant knowledge,' raising doubt that gains stem from genuine forgetting rather than a regularization/noise effect; baselines are not clearly controlled for training steps or compute.
justification: Sec 3.3 confirms the forget sets (BC-Select, BC-Mixed, BC-Cosine) are all built from BookCorpus with only ~100-1000 samples, and the paper reports no compute/step-matched comparison against SFT/DAPT/LoRA/CurlLoRA baselines.

weakness: Gains from F2F are inconsistent across model scales (large on Qwen-0.6B, more moderate on LLaMA-8B) and Gemma-2B shows catastrophic degradation after the unlearning step (HumanEval 0.00) with only small net improvement, yet the paper offers no rigorous explanation beyond vague appeals to 'model capacity.'
justification: Table 1 shows Gemma HumanEval drops to 0.00 after Unl_GA+GD and the paper's explanation is only the qualitative statement that 'aggressive unlearning may overwhelm models with limited capacity,' without further rigorous analysis, matching the review's claim.

weakness: Key experimental details are missing: the number of unlearning steps/epochs is not reported, and it's unclear how the retain set (a 'small subset of the fine-tuning data') is chosen and whether it overlaps with the evaluation/test data.
justification: Section 2 describes running the unlearn loop for 'T_u steps' without ever giving a concrete value in the main text, and Sec 3.3 only vaguely states the retain set is 'a small subset of the fine-tuning data' without specifying the selection procedure or confirming no overlap with test sets.

weakness: The paper overclaims novelty by calling itself 'the first comprehensive study' of unlearning for domain specialization, when prior work (e.g., Chen et al. 2023a on active forgetting during pretraining) touches on related ideas.
justification: The paper itself cites Chen et al. (2023a) as having shown 'active forgetting mechanism during pre-training led to faster convergence and better low-resource adaptation,' which is closely related prior art that tempers the 'first' claim even though the paper's post-hoc fine-tuning framing differs somewhat.

weakness: The CKA/SVCCA representation analysis is limited to a single model size/architecture, so it's unclear whether the observed geometric shifts generalize across all tested models.
justification: Section 4.5/Figures 4-5 present CKA and SVCCA results without indicating they were repeated across the five different model families and sizes used in Table 1, so generalization of the representational-geometry finding is unverified.

weakness: Table 3 is large and difficult to parse, with unclear headers for forget-set type and model.
justification: Table 3 packs 3 models x 3 forget-set variants x 2 unlearning methods x 6 metrics into one dense table with repeated unlabeled row groups, making it genuinely hard to parse as described.

weakness: No empirical evaluation: the paper contains zero experiments despite referencing GRAAL's practical results.
justification: The paper text (abstract through appendix-cut section 4.2) contains no experimental section at all, only theoretical algorithm and proofs, confirming the absence of empirical validation.

weakness: Parameter selection is unclear: the algorithm requires parameters θ, γ, ν satisfying condition (19), but the paper only states 'it is easy to verify that such parameters exist' without giving concrete values or a constructive procedure.
justification: Section 2.2 (Theorem 1) states parameters must satisfy eq. (19) and says only 'it is easy to verify that such parameters exist,' with no example values or explicit construction procedure given anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: Computational cost per iteration is not discussed: computing λ_{k+1} requires evaluating Λ at multiple points, and the paper never analyzes whether this per-iteration overhead compared to standard AGD is justified.
justification: The algorithm (Algorithm 1, line 10) does require multiple Λ evaluations per iteration, and no part of the paper text discusses per-iteration computational cost or overhead relative to AGD.

weakness: The complexity result for (L0,L1)-smooth functions has an additive term (L1D)^3, which is worse than Vankov et al.'s (L1D)^{5/3} and Tyurin's (L1D)^2.
justification: Table 1 in the paper itself confirms Corollary 3 gives (L1D)^3 versus (L1D)^{5/3} for Vankov et al. and (L1D)^2 for Tyurin, exactly as the reviewer states.

weakness: The condition η0 L0 exp(L1||x0-x*||) ≤ 1 requires the initial stepsize to be exponentially small, which may lead to very slow initial progress, and choosing η0=10^-10 could result in a large additive logarithmic term.
justification: The paper explicitly addresses and rebuts this exact concern, stating that choosing η0 very small 'will only result in a small logarithmic additive factor... which does not depend on the precision ε,' so the reviewer's framing of this as an unaddressed problem overlooks the paper's own justification.

weakness: No physical-world evaluation: attack and defense are validated only in the LIBERO simulation benchmark, without any physical robot experiments or sim-to-real transfer analysis, despite the stated motivation for patch attacks being physical deployability.
justification: The paper's experiments section (4.1-4.3) only describes LIBERO simulation evaluations, and the Limitation section (Section 6) does not mention any physical-world validation, confirming this gap.

weakness: Defense evaluation only on OpenVLA: the adversarial fine-tuning defense is evaluated solely on OpenVLA, raising questions about transferability to OpenVLA-OFT and π₀.
justification: Section 4.2/4.3 confirms defense results are only reported for OpenVLA (Table 2); Table 3 for other VLAs only reports attack, not defense, results.

weakness: Lack of detailed comparison with potential alternative defenses: the proposed defense is compared only against the pre-attack baseline, with no comparison to standard adversarial training, certified defenses, or preprocessing defenses.
justification: Table 2 compares only Original vs. Adversarial Finetuned performance; no other defense baselines (certified defense, input preprocessing, etc.) are evaluated anywhere in the paper.

weakness: Patch placement strategy not specified: the paper does not discuss where in the image the patch is placed (fixed, random, or optimized), which limits reproducibility.
justification: Equation 1 and the hyperparameter settings only specify patch size (50x50) but never describe placement location or strategy anywhere in the provided methodology or experimental sections.

weakness: Limited analysis of the trade-off between attack objectives: the paper does not provide ablation studies showing how different α₁ values affect attack success.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'The sensitivity to some of these hyperparameter settings are reported in Appendix C,' so an ablation analysis exists in the appendix, which the reviewer overlooked.

weakness: Only one baseline comparison for multi-camera models: for OpenVLA-OFT and π₀, EDPA is only compared against random noise and clean conditions without UADA/UPA.
justification: Section 4.3 explicitly confirms UADA and UPA are excluded from multi-camera comparisons due to transfer difficulty, leaving only random noise/clean baselines as stated.

weakness: The paper would benefit from error bars in Figure 2 patch visualizations.
justification: Figure 2 as described in the paper shows only qualitative patch images without any quantitative/statistical annotation, supporting this minor point.

weakness: Some cited references in the ethics statement are not fully listed (e.g., UADA and UPA citations omitted).
justification: The Ethics Statement discusses adversarial patches generally without inline citations to Wang et al. (2024)/UADA/UPA, consistent with the reviewer's observation.

weakness: Privacy analysis is not rigorous — no formal privacy definition (e.g., DP), Lemma 2 depends on an unspecified/hard-to-evaluate Lipschitz constant, and the 'uniform privacy protection' claim (Remark 3) is not mathematically supported.
justification: The paper indeed never states a formal (epsilon,delta)-DP-style guarantee, only reconstruction-error bounds (Lemmas 1-2) that depend on an unspecified Lipschitz constant L_v(x), so the critique is well grounded.

weakness: Theorem 2's convergence bound mixes a high-probability statement with expectations in a non-standard way, and the epsilon-dependence is not clearly resolved into a clean rate.
justification: Theorem 2 as quoted does state 'with probability at least 1-delta' while the bound itself is written as an expectation sum containing an O(epsilon G^2/K^0.5) term without specifying how epsilon is fixed relative to K, supporting the reviewer's point.

weakness: Multi-round privacy composition (Remark 2) is only heuristically addressed; the T×m<d bound is weak and not a rigorous composition analysis for realistic (non-static) gradients.
justification: Remark 2 explicitly says the bound holds 'even in a worst-case scenario (e.g., a static gradient)' and offers no formal analysis for evolving gradients beyond an informal note that 'natural evolution... provides stronger practical protection', matching the critique.

weakness: No experimental comparison with methods that jointly handle compression and differential privacy (e.g., CP-SGD, Amiri et al. 2021, Lyu 2021), even though they are cited.
justification: The related work section discusses Amiri et al. and Lyu et al. only conceptually; the experiments section (Tables 1-2) only compares against sketching/structured/top-k/QSGD baselines, not these DP+compression methods.

weakness: Only two gradient inversion attacks (Yu et al. 2025 and DLG) were used to validate privacy; more established attacks should be considered.
justification: The reviewer does not specify which additional established attacks are needed or why the recent SOTA GIA plus the classic DLG method are insufficient; this is a generic, unspecific ask rather than a concrete, paper-specific gap.

weakness: The claim that computational cost (Remark 1) is 'negligible' is not backed by wall-clock timing experiments.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'as reported in Table A.10 for one representative experiment, this computational time is negligible and does not constitute a bottleneck in our experiments,' indicating timing data does exist, which the reviewer overlooked.

weakness: The privacy-communication trade-off (varying m) is not systematically demonstrated with a wide sweep of m values against accuracy/communication/SSIM.
justification: The paper states 'In Table A.9 of Appendix A, we present experiments over a wide range of m values to further illustrate the findings of Theorem 2,' directly contradicting the reviewer's claim that no such sweep exists.

weakness: Definition 1 defines the projected directional derivative for a scalar function f, but the same term is later used for the stochastic gradient estimator, creating notational inconsistency.
justification: Definition 1 is stated for a differentiable function f:R^d->R, while Section 2 and Algorithm 2 apply the same terminology to per-client stochastic gradients g_i(x_k), a genuine notational overload in the paper.

weakness: The contribution-statement formula ĝ_i(x_k) = U_{k,i} g_i(x_k) U_{k,i} is mathematically invalid (matrix times vector times matrix); it should be (1/m)U_{k,i}U_{k,i}^T g_i(x_k).
justification: This exact expression appears verbatim in the Statement of Contribution paragraph of the paper and is dimensionally inconsistent, confirming the reviewer's specific, checkable notational error.

weakness: The claim to be the first to introduce the projected directional derivative in FL should be toned down since random-projection-based compression (e.g., Count-Sketch, random rotation) is well known.
justification: The paper already scopes its novelty claim precisely to 'the first work to introduce the projected directional derivative in FL, specifically through a novel multi-projection decomposition,' not to random projections in general, so the criticism mischaracterizes the paper's actual claim.

weakness: The c_dec metric is not a perfect guide: it can remain nearly flat over a wide L0 range and the 'elbow' heuristic is somewhat ad-hoc, requiring subjective judgment; the paper would benefit from a more principled way to identify correct L0.
justification: The paper itself acknowledges this in the Discussion: 'we do not view this as a perfect guide... the metric can sometime remain nearly flat for a wide range of L0,' matching the review's critique.

weakness: The proposed method requires an expensive L0 sweep (training multiple SAEs, e.g. 500M tokens per SAE), and automatic optimization of c_dec during training is only discussed in an appendix but not implemented or validated, limiting practical utility.
justification: The paper confirms LLM SAEs were trained on 500M tokens each across a sweep of L0 values (Section 4), and the Discussion states the automatic optimization 'is left to future work' without implementation.

weakness: Limited theoretical justification for c_dec: the formal justification in Appendix A.6 is brief and relies on simplifying assumptions such as orthogonal true features.
justification: The toy models explicitly assume orthogonal features ('All features are orthogonal, so f_i . f_j = 0'), so the theoretical grounding indeed rests on this simplifying assumption; the paper only references the formal justification without including it in the main text.

weakness: The paper's findings and c_dec metric are only validated on BatchTopK and JumpReLU SAEs; it is unclear whether the results extend to other popular architectures like Gated SAEs or standard L1 SAEs, which are mentioned in the background but not tested.
justification: The paper explicitly states 'In this work we focus on BatchTopK and JumpReLU SAEs' and later 'So far, we have only investigated BatchTopK SAEs... We now validate that these same conclusions apply to JumpReLU SAEs,' with L1 SAEs mentioned only in Background (Section 2) and never tested.

weakness: The evidence for the claim that most commonly used SAEs have too low L0 is only a 'cursory search of open source SAEs on Neuronpedia' (Appendix A.13), which is not a systematic or quantitative survey.
justification: The paper's own Discussion section uses the phrase 'a cursory search of open source SAEs on Neuronpedia (Lin, 2023) shows L0 less than 100 is very common,' confirming the review's characterization of this evidence as informal.

weakness: Limited scope of the dissipative use-case: the heat transfer system is only 2-dimensional, limiting the strength of the 'smaller models' claim; scaling to higher-dimensional dissipative systems would strengthen the paper.
justification: The paper's dissipative case study is indeed restricted to a 2-state heat transfer LSSM (Section 2.1, m=2 states), so this is a real scope limitation.

weakness: Unclear novelty of the heat transfer approach: using Riemannian optimization (RAdam) to enforce SPD constraints is a fairly standard application of known techniques, and the paper does not clearly articulate novelty beyond applying RAdam to this specific problem.
justification: The paper explicitly states it adopts RAdam from Bécigneul & Ganea (2019) via the geoopt library, and frames the contribution as a case study/demonstration rather than a new optimization method, supporting this critique.

weakness: Missing implementation details for SPD optimization: the specific Riemannian metric (e.g., affine-invariant, Log-Euclidean) and how the exponential/log maps are computed are not specified beyond the general equation.
justification: Section 2.1.1/2.1.2 describes the log/exp maps abstractly and cites geoopt, but never states which Riemannian metric is used for the SPD manifold, so this reproducibility gap is real.

weakness: Questionable fairness in baseline comparisons: the EucOpt baseline is not constrained to be SPD, making it an unfair comparison for isolating whether structure (vs. optimization scheme) helps; a Cholesky-parameterized Euclidean LSSM baseline is mentioned but not actually compared.
justification: The paper mentions the Cholesky parameterization as 'an alternative approach' but never reports results for it, and describes EucOpt only as using Euclidean gradient updates without stating it is SPD-constrained, confirming the gap.

weakness: The 'smaller models' claim is not rigorously quantified: Figure 3/Table 2 show SHNN test and rollout MSE continuing to improve with size, and the paper doesn't discuss whether a saturation point or fundamentally different scaling exponent exists.
justification: Table 2 shows SHNN Test_MSE and Drift_RMS both generally decreasing as L and W increase, and the paper does not analyze scaling trends/saturation, so this critique is grounded in the actual reported numbers.

weakness: The FPUT unseen initial condition test only evaluates a single unseen initial condition; testing on a distribution of unseen conditions would be more convincing than a single-trajectory chronological split.
justification: Section 3.2 describes a single simulated trajectory split chronologically for train/test, and Figures 4b/4c show only one unseen initial condition trajectory, confirming this limitation (the 'data leakage' framing is loose but the underlying limited-IC-testing point is accurate).

weakness: Missing error bars/statistical significance: Tables 1 and 2 report single values without standard deviations or multiple seeds.
justification: Table 1 and Table 2 in the paper report single point-estimate MSE/drift values with no mention of repeated runs or confidence intervals anywhere in the text.

weakness: The heat transfer results are mixed: RieOpt is not uniformly better than XGBoost, e.g., XGBoost has better MSE on T_ext2 for London, and the paper doesn't discuss this nuance.
justification: Table 1 shows XGBoost at 1.06e-01 vs RieOpt at 5.07e-01 for T_ext2/London, confirming RieOpt is not uniformly best, and the results section focuses on RieOpt's wins without addressing this exception.

weakness: The paper occasionally uses imprecise/informal language (e.g., 'nudging' for Riemannian optimization) that could be clarified for precision.
justification: This is a subjective stylistic nitpick without specifying which passages are actually confusing or how they impede understanding, similar to vague typo/wording critiques flagged as unreliable in the guideline.

weakness: Limited novelty beyond integration of existing components; ablation shows bulk of accuracy gain comes from pre-trained QA-Token vocabulary, not HighClass's own design decisions.
justification: The paper itself states QA-Token, MetaTrinity architecture, and sparsification are 'synthesized' from prior works, and Table 3 confirms the 6.8pp gain over k-mers comes from the vocabulary.

weakness: Theoretical contribution is incremental (standard Rademacher complexity, well-known concentration/consistency techniques), and 'first comprehensive theory' claim is overstated.
justification: The paper's Theorem 6/Lemma 7/Theorem 8 do use standard Rademacher complexity, α-mixing concentration, and MLE consistency techniques applied to a new setting, supporting the incrementality claim.

weakness: Insufficient comparison with modern baselines: only MetaTrinity (2023) is the SOTA comparator; Kraken2/Centrifuge are older; no KrakenUniq, Bracken, or deep learning baselines.
justification: Section 5.3 confirms comparisons only against MetaTrinity, Kraken2 (2019), and Centrifuge (2016) with no other modern methods included.

weakness: Inconsistency with reported QA-Token accuracy (0.917 F1) vs HighClass's 85.1%, and paper doesn't adequately discuss why hash-mapping can't match QA-Token alone's accuracy.
justification: Table 3 and Section 2.1 confirm the 0.917 vs 0.862/0.851 gap, and the paper only briefly attributes it to the alignment-to-hash-lookup trade-off without deeper analysis of when this trade-off is favorable.

weakness: Dependence on external pre-trained resources (QA-Token vocabularies, sparsification masks) makes it hard to assess intrinsic contribution.
justification: Reproducibility statement explicitly confirms use of pre-trained QA-Token vocabularies and pre-computed sparsification masks from other works.

weakness: Limited dataset results in main text: only CAMI II Marine results shown despite mentioning CAMI II Strain, HMP, Zymo benchmarks.
justification: Section 5.3 lists CAMI II Marine, Strain, HMP, and Zymo as evaluation benchmarks, but all main tables (2,3,4,5,6) report only CAMI II Marine results.

weakness: Claims of surpassing stronger models are nuanced and context-dependent; e.g., on TSP in-domain (N=50), the GPT-4o-mini variant of CALM (without RL) achieves 10.54% gap versus MCTS-AHD's 9.69%, slightly worse, so the paper's blanket claim of surpassing API-based methods should be more precisely characterized.
justification: Table 2 confirms CALM (API, w/o GRPO) at N=50 has 10.54% gap vs MCTS-AHD's 9.69%, a real exception to the paper's broad claim of surpassing verbal-only methods with more powerful models.

weakness: Statistical significance is not reported in the main paper; results are means over 3 runs without standard deviations or confidence intervals, even though some performance gaps between CALM and top baselines are modest.
justification: The paper states p-values and statistical significance analyses are only in Appendix I ('statistical significance (p-values)'), confirming they are absent from the main text tables.

weakness: The framework has many components (5 operators, collapse mechanism with two hyperparameters, reward function with multiple scalars) and the ablation shows some collapse hyperparameter choices substantially degrade performance, yet the practical challenge of tuning these hyperparameters is underemphasized in the main text.
justification: Table 4 shows δ0=0.005, C=15 gives 27.22% on OP versus 17.41% default, a large degradation, and the main text gives only brief discussion without a dedicated sensitivity analysis in the main paper (noted as being in the appendix).

weakness: The API-based variant comparison ('Efficacy of verbal gradient') is somewhat asymmetric because it changes the backend to GPT-4o-mini, sets G=1, and uses a different query budget, conflating model capability with prompt design rather than isolating the verbal gradient operators alone.
justification: Section 5.2 explicitly describes switching backend, setting G=1, and using T=4000/2000 matching prior methods' budgets, which indeed changes multiple factors simultaneously rather than isolating the verbal-gradient design against a matched Qwen2.5 baseline without RL.

weakness: Limited discussion of potential overfitting or distribution shift during fine-tuning, since the LLM is continuously fine-tuned on responses generated from prompts seen during the search, and the paper does not discuss whether the LLM overfits to the specific prompt distribution.
justification: The paper describes the GRPO fine-tuning loop in detail (Sections 3.2, 4) but nowhere addresses overfitting to the prompt distribution or its effect on generalization across tasks/trajectories, matching the reviewer's claim of a genuine gap.

weakness: Limited problem scale: all experiments are on relatively small-scale problems and the paper does not demonstrate scalability to higher-dimensional or more complex instances.
justification: All benchmarks reported (2D functions, small polynomial systems like katsura10/cyclic7, 10D funnel, 4-particle DW-4) are indeed small/low-dimensional, and there is no experiment on larger-scale instances in the paper.

weakness: State computation overhead (convergence velocity, e.g. KSD) is not accounted for in runtime comparisons, potentially overstating efficiency gains.
justification: The paper defines convergence velocity as requiring objective/KSD computation but never discusses or subtracts this overhead from the reported Time columns in Tables 1-5.

weakness: Reward design sensitivity: no analysis of how λ1, λ2 affect the learned policy or robustness across problem classes.
justification: The paper only states λ1, λ2 are 'scaling coefficients detailed in Appendix A' with no sensitivity analysis in the main text (and the visible portion gives no such analysis).

weakness: Incomparable baselines: runtime comparisons against Simulator HC (C++) and iDEM (more powerful GPU) are explicitly marked not directly comparable, yet still used to support efficiency claims.
justification: The paper itself states these caveats in footnotes ('Runtimes are not directly comparable...') while still presenting them in the main efficiency narrative.

weakness: Neural network capacity: the policy network is a small MLP (2 layers, 16 units), unclear if it generalizes to more complex homotopy landscapes.
justification: Confirmed by paper's implementation details (MLP with two hidden layers of 16 units); no evidence given about scaling to more complex landscapes.

weakness: Generalization scope: training is done on a single instance or narrow distribution, and the paper does not test generalization to substantially different problem distributions within the same class.
justification: Training sets described (Aquarius sequence, Ackley with randomized parameters, 4-view triangulation, 10-mode GMM) are narrow, and no broader distribution-shift generalization test is reported.

weakness: No failure case analysis: paper reports 100% success for HC but does not discuss scenarios where NPC might fail or compare failure modes with classical methods.
justification: Table 4 shows 100% success rates with no discussion of failure conditions or ill-conditioned trajectories anywhere in the visible text.

weakness: Hyperparameter reporting: reward coefficients λ1, λ2 are only referenced to Appendix A, not given in main text.
justification: Confirmed: the paper states 'λ1, λ2 are scaling coefficients detailed in Appendix A' without giving values in the main text.

weakness: The term 'Homotopy' is capitalized inconsistently in the title and body.
justification: The title uses 'HOMO-TOPY' (all caps) while body text mixes 'Homotopy paradigm' and lowercase 'homotopy', confirming inconsistent capitalization.

weakness: Limited validation on a single K562 CRISPRi Perturb-seq dataset; needs additional datasets covering different cell types, perturbation modalities, and sequencing technologies to establish generalizability.
justification: The paper's own Conclusion admits this limitation: 'Larger atlases such as the Human Cell Atlas... will be necessary to test scalability... Generalizability to other ontologies and modalities' are listed as future work, confirming only one dataset was used.
